Rust at work, part 1 of 4

Your first three weeks at Kettle Creek Supply

You have just started at Kettle Creek Supply, a distributor of bearings, bolts, hoses and other industrial parts. Your title says analyst. The job is writing software. Your manager will email you work, and each request needs a little more Rust than the last. This page teaches exactly that much, just before you need it. You write all the code yourself, in your own editor. When a ticket is done, a senior engineer reviews it the way a pull request is reviewed at a well-run company: what is wrong, what is unclear, and what will hurt in six months.

What you need. Rust 1.89 or newer (cargo --version), git, an editor with rust-analyzer (Neovim or VS Code, both covered in set up), Claude Code for the reviews (it never writes your code; set up shows how to tell it so), an internet connection for the first build, and the practice database, kettle_creek.db (in the course repository it's data/kettle_creek.db, and python3 data/make_db.py rebuilds it).

What you have at the end of part 1. A tested Rust codebase of about a thousand lines, split into modules, that you wrote and can defend line by line. It reads the warehouse database, reconciles invoices against purchase orders, parses dirty data without crashing, and produces the monthly Excel pack for finance. Every program, output and compiler error on this page was run before it was written down.

How to work a ticket.

  1. Read the email. Before scrolling, write three lines in your journal: what you think the program needs to do, and what you don't know how to do yet.
  2. Read the wiki page under it. That is the "just enough Rust" for this ticket. Type the examples, don't paste them: your fingers learn shapes that your eyes skim over.
  3. Do the warm-up drills. They're small practice on the same ideas, and from ticket 1 on they use the real database. Some take ten minutes, and the later ones can take an evening.
  4. Read "Under the hood". It isn't optional: it explains why the Rust works the way it does, later tickets assume you've read it, and the quiz asks about it. The history in it (calendars, old papers) can be read lightly. The parts a ticket leans on are linked from its "Before you type" questions.
  5. Build the ticket. Open a hint only after twenty minutes of being properly stuck.
  6. Run the sanity checks, commit, and ask for a review.
  7. Fix what the review finds, yourself, and take the quiz. "Go deeper" is for when you want more.

How this works

Kettle Creek Supply buys parts from two dozen suppliers and sells them to factories and repair shops. Purchasing raises a purchase order (PO) for each order: what it bought, how many and at what price. The supplier ships the parts and later sends an invoice, which says how much to pay. Most of the work in this course comes from a single question that every distributor asks: did we pay what we agreed to pay?

The company is invented and so is every row of its data. The work is real. Reconciling invoices, cleaning a newly acquired branch's records, building a scheduled job and putting an API in front of it are things people get paid to do, and they need the same skills here as they do in a real job.

Who's who

WhoWhat they want from you
Dana Whitlock, Operations ManagerYour manager. Writes the tickets. Cares whether the answer is right and on time, not how the code looks.
Priya Raman, Accounts Payable leadFinance. Pays the suppliers. Cares about every cent, and appears from ticket 2.
The senior engineerReviews your code when a ticket is done. In practice this is Claude, run from your terminal, under rules that stop it writing your code. See How reviews work.

House rules

These are the rules a good engineering team would give a new hire. Each one is here because breaking it costs you something later.

  1. You write every line. Claude can explain a compiler error, point you at a concept, or review finished work. It does not write your implementation. The CLAUDE.md you add during set up tells it so.
  2. SQL stops at SELECT columns FROM table. No WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY or SUM. Kettle Creek's IT team asks for this because business rules buried in SQL strings inside a program are easy to miss in review, awkward to test without a live database, and soon forgotten. For you there is a second reason: every filter, join and total you write in Rust is Rust you learn.
  3. No crate until a ticket needs it. Each ticket names the crates it allows. Learning what the standard library already does is part of the job.
  4. Clean before review. cargo fmt, then cargo clippy --all-targets with no warnings, then cargo test. A reviewer's time goes on design, not on things a tool can find.
  5. Commit each ticket, and say why. A commit message says what changed and why it changed. Tag the commit you hand in, so the review can see exactly what changed since the last ticket.
  6. Keep a journal. Three lines per ticket in JOURNAL.md: what surprised you, what the compiler taught you, and what you would design differently. Writing it down is what turns an error you fixed into one you won't make again.

The whole road

The codebase grows with you. You won't design a big system up front; each new request pushes the existing code until it needs a better shape, and that's when you learn the shape. Part 1 is written and on this page. Later parts get written when you reach them, so they can push on whatever your reviews show you need.

Set up

Do this before week zero. The point is a project you can build, a loop you can run in your sleep, and the rules written down where Claude will read them.

Check your tools

cargo --version
rustup component list --installed
claude --version

You want cargo 1.89 or newer (rustup update gets it) and, in the component list, clippy, rustfmt and rust-analyzer. On this machine all three are installed. The last line checks for Claude Code, the command-line Claude that does your reviews. If it's missing, Anthropic's Claude Code documentation says how to install it.

Make the project

cd ~/projects
cargo new kettle_creek
cd kettle_creek
mkdir data out
cp ~/projects/space_sim/learning/data/kettle_creek.db data/   # or wherever your copy is
cargo add rusqlite --features bundled
printf '/out\n/data/*.db\n' >> .gitignore

cargo new makes Cargo.toml, src/main.rs and a git repository with a .gitignore that already skips target/. The last line adds two more: your program's output files, which are rebuilt every run, and your copy of the database, which you can always copy again. printf prints the text, with \n as a line break, and >> adds it to the end of the file. A single > would replace the file instead.

Because out/ is ignored, git never stores it, and a fresh clone of your project won't have one. Writing to out/report.csv then fails with No such file or directory, a message that doesn't say which path. So have your program make the folder before it writes there: std::fs::create_dir_all("out")? creates it, and does nothing if it already exists.

cargo add rusqlite --features bundled adds the SQLite crate. A crate is one unit of compiled Rust, a library or a program, and a package is what cargo downloads and builds, holding one or more crates. Day to day, people say crate for both. bundled compiles SQLite itself from C source into your program, so SQLite doesn't have to be installed on the machine. It does need a C compiler. On Linux and macOS, Rust normally links programs through the system's C toolchain, so you usually have one already. If the first build fails with an error that mentions cc, install your system's C build tools and try again. That makes the first build slow, a minute or so, and every build after it fast. Cargo.toml now ends with something like:

[dependencies]
rusqlite = { version = "0.40.2", features = ["bundled"] }

Your version may be newer. If an example on this page stops compiling with a newer rusqlite, pin the tested one with version = "=0.40.2".

The database

The file is a copy of the warehouse system's tables, as of Monday, October 5, 2026. Dates are text in YYYY-MM-DD form. Money is stored the way many real systems store it, as floating-point dollars in a REAL column, and ticket 3 is about why that is a problem.

TableRowsColumns
suppliers24supplier_id, name, city, state, payment_terms_days, active (1 or 0)
products176sku, description, category, supplier_id, list_price
purchase_orders2,017po_id, supplier_id, branch (MAIN or MILLBROOK), buyer, order_date, expected_date, received_date (empty until the parts arrive), status (open, received or cancelled)
po_lines5,315po_id, line_no, sku, quantity, unit_price
invoices1,745invoice_id, invoice_number, supplier_id, po_id, invoice_date, amount
branch_invoices183All text, no rules. You meet it in ticket 4.

To look around, install the sqlite3 command-line program from your package manager (the bundled feature puts SQLite inside your program, not on your machine). Then sqlite3 data/kettle_creek.db opens a prompt. .tables lists tables, .schema purchase_orders shows one, and SELECT * FROM suppliers LIMIT 5; shows a few rows. Using SQL to look is fine. The rule is about what goes in your program.

The loop you'll run a thousand times

CommandWhat it doesPython's nearest
cargo checkType-checks without building a program. Fastest way to see errors.mypy, a type checker for Python, if you've used one
cargo runBuilds, then runs src/main.rs. Arguments after -- go to your program.python main.py
cargo clippy --all-targetsThe linter: hundreds of checks for code that works but could be clearer, faster or more correct.ruff or pylint, the Python tools that flag code that runs but looks wrong
cargo fmtFormats every file the one standard way. Nobody argues about style in Rust.black
cargo testBuilds and runs every test. From ticket 4.pytest

Your editor

Whatever editor you use, it should run rust-analyzer, the program that reads your code as you type and shows errors, types and docs in place. Without it you find every mistake at the next cargo build, and Rust is much harder to learn that way.

Your Neovim already runs rust-analyzer through rustaceanvim, with clippy on every save, and shows inferred types as gray inlay hints. Start nvim from the project folder so it picks up the right project. The keys worth learning this week, all from your own config. <leader> is the prefix key your config sets. With a different Neovim setup the keys will differ, and the actions are what to look for:

KeyWhat it does
KHover: the type and docs of whatever is under the cursor. Use it constantly.
gdGo to definition, including into a crate's source. Reading library code is how you learn idioms.
<leader>cdShow this line's problems in a float.
<leader>rdThe full compiler message, laid out the way cargo build prints it. Read this rather than the one-line summary.
<leader>reExplain the error code, the same text as rustc --explain.
<leader>roOpen the docs page for the symbol under the cursor.
<leader>rr, <leader>rtRun the program, run tests.
<leader>xxEvery problem in the project, as a list.

If you'd rather use VS Code, install the rust-analyzer extension (from the rust-lang publisher) and open the project folder, not a single file. Then set rust-analyzer.check.command to clippy in the settings, so you see clippy's warnings on every save. The same jobs, VS Code's way:

KeyWhat it does
Hover with the mouse, or Ctrl+K Ctrl+IThe type and docs of whatever is under the cursor.
F12Go to definition, including into a crate's source.
Ctrl+Shift+MThe Problems panel: every error and warning in the project. Click one to jump to it.
Ctrl+.Quick fixes for the problem under the cursor, often the compiler's own suggestion.
The "Run" and "Debug" linksrust-analyzer puts them above fn main and above each test.

On a Mac, Ctrl is Cmd. The full compiler message is always in the terminal: when the editor's one-line summary isn't enough, run cargo build and read it there. Where this page names a Neovim key, the VS Code row above does the same job.

How to read a compiler error

Rust's compiler is the best teacher you'll have, if you read what it says. Here is a small mistake and the message it produces. You don't need to type this one: it's the kind of error you'll meet in ticket 1, in the kettle_creek project, so the last line names that project. Errors in snippets name snippets.

fn main() {
    let words = vec!["pear", "fig"];
    words.push("kiwi");
    println!("{words:?}");
}
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `words` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     words.push("kiwi");
  |     ^^^^^ cannot borrow as mutable
  |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
  |
2 |     let mut words = vec!["pear", "fig"];
  |         +++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0596`.
error: could not compile `kettle_creek` (bin "kettle_creek") due to 1 previous error
  • The first line is the headline: an error code (E0596) and a sentence. The code is a search term: rustc --explain E0596 prints a page about it with examples.
  • The arrow (--> src/main.rs:3:5) is the file, line and column.
  • The carets (^^^^^) underline the exact code, with a label saying what is wrong there.
  • The help is a suggested fix, and the +++ marks what it would add. It is right most of the time. When it isn't, it still tells you what the compiler expected.

Fix the first error, then rebuild. One mistake often causes several errors further down, and they disappear with the first.

Tell Claude the rules

Save this as CLAUDE.md in the project root. Claude Code reads it at the start of every session in that folder, so the rules hold even when you ask for help late at night and would secretly like the answer.

# kettle_creek

My Rust learning project. I am working through the guide at
~/projects/space_sim/learning/rust_at_work.html, one ticket at a time.

## Rules for Claude

- Never write or edit code in this project, even if I ask casually.
  Never show me a full solution to a ticket.
- If I'm stuck, ask what I tried, then give the smallest hint that
  unblocks me: a concept name, a docs link, or a short example on
  different data. Suggest the next rung of the guide's hint ladder
  before going further.
- Explaining compiler errors is encouraged: what the message means and
  what Rust is protecting me from. Let me write the fix.
- When I ask for a senior review, follow "How reviews work" in the
  guide: run the checks, compare my output with the answer key, then
  review like a senior engineer on a pull request. Don't rewrite it.
- The answer key is in ~/projects/testRandomShiz/rust_at_work/answer_key.
  Never show me its code or open its output files for me. You may compare
  my output with it and tell me where they differ.

Then start the journal and make the first commit:

printf '# Journal\n\n' > JOURNAL.md
cargo run
git add -A
git commit -m "Start kettle_creek: empty binary, rusqlite, rules for Claude"

git add -A stages every change: it marks what goes into the next commit. git commit then saves the staged changes as one snapshot you can always get back to. If this is the first time you've used git on this machine, the commit stops and asks who you are. Tell it once, with your own name and email, and commit again:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

If cargo run prints Hello, world! after compiling SQLite, you're set up. Week zero is next.

How reviews work

A review is where most of the learning in this course happens. Getting a program to print the right number is half the job. The other half is a program that the next person, or you in six months, can read, change and trust. Nobody can teach you that half from a book. It comes from someone looking at your code and asking why.

When to ask

When the sanity checks pass, cargo fmt and cargo clippy --all-targets are clean, and the work is committed and tagged:

git add -A
git commit -m "Ticket 1: count open POs and list stale ones"
git tag t1-submitted

A tag is a name stuck on one commit, so you and the reviewer can say "the code as handed in" without copying a commit's long ID. git tag lists them, and git diff t1-final t2-submitted shows everything that changed between two of them. A tag stays on its commit when you commit again. If you fix something before the review and want to hand in the new version, move the tag with git tag -f t1-submitted; without -f, git says the tag already exists.

What to paste

Start claude in the project folder and paste this, with the ticket number filled in. Each ticket adds a line or two of its own to focus the review.

Senior review, ticket N.

My code is in this folder; the tag tN-submitted is what I'm handing in,
and the ticket is the "Ticket N" section of
~/projects/space_sim/learning/rust_at_work.html.

1. Run cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets and cargo test,
   then run the program the way the ticket asks.
2. Compare my output files with the answer key's
   (~/projects/testRandomShiz/rust_at_work/answer_key/out/tN/).
   Tell me whether they match. If not, tell me which rows or numbers
   differ, but not why. Free-text columns (like a reject reason) only
   have to mean the same thing, not match word for word.
3. Review it like a senior engineer reviewing a pull request:
   correctness, structure and file layout, naming, error handling,
   ownership, idiomatic Rust and tests. At most seven points, most
   important first. For each one: file and line, what's wrong, why it
   matters, and the concept or docs page to look up.
4. Don't rewrite my code or show me a fixed version. A short example on
   different data is fine.
5. End with one thing I did well, and one question for my journal.

What the reviewer looks for

The same list every time. Read it before you start a ticket, not just before you hand it in.

AreaThe question
CorrectDoes it do what the ticket says, including the edge cases the email mentions in passing?
ClearDoes main read like a summary of the program? Does each function do one thing its name describes?
StructuredIs each file about one thing? Is the structure as simple as the problem allows, and no simpler?
Honest about failureCan bad data or a missing file crash it? When it fails, does the message say what went wrong and where?
OwnershipDoes it borrow by default, and clone only on purpose?
IdiomaticIterators where they read better than loops, the standard library's types instead of homemade ones, derive instead of hand-written boilerplate.
TestedFrom ticket 4: would a test fail if the important logic broke?
ReproducibleSame input, same output, byte for byte. No absolute paths baked in.

After the review

Fix what it found, yourself. If you disagree with a point, say so and ask for the tradeoff. A good reviewer can tell you what the alternative costs, and sometimes your way is fine. Then write your journal lines, commit, and git tag tN-final. The next ticket starts from there.

Welcome, and one thing before Monday

We're all looking forward to Monday. IT says your laptop is set up and Rust is installed.

See you Monday, Dana

This page teaches what compiling is, how a Rust program is laid out, variables and number types, macros and formatting, dbg!, loops and conditions, tuples, arrays, vectors and slices, references, functions, structs with methods, Option and Result, closures and iterator methods, imports, how to read the docs, and when to distrust the compiler's suggestions. Under the hood: how integers are stored, what memory is, how text becomes bytes, and what a process is. Crates allowed: none.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Start here

Rust from the ground up

This page assumes you can program in Python and have never had to think about what happens underneath. Each new word is in italics where it's first explained, and the machine words (memory, addresses, processes) get a fuller explanation in under the hood at the end. Where Python does the same thing differently, the page says so, because the differences are where your instincts will mislead you.

You need a scratch project to type examples into. Make one next to where your work project will go:

cd ~/projects
cargo new snippets
cd snippets
cargo run

It prints Hello, world!. Type each example on this page into src/main.rs and run it with cargo run. An example with its own fn main is a whole program: replace everything in the file. An example without one is a piece. Lines that start with let, or that do something, go inside main, between fn main() { and its closing brace. Definitions (use, const, struct, impl, fn) go above main. Within one subsection, later pieces can use names from earlier ones, so keep the earlier lines, except a line that panics on purpose: delete that once you've seen it, or nothing after it will run. Type them, don't paste: your fingers learn the shapes that your eyes skim over. Ticket 1 adds a database library to this same project later.

What cargo run actually does

When you run python report.py, Python checks that the file is valid syntax, then carries out each line as it reaches it. A misspelled name or a wrong type on line 40 isn't noticed until line 40 runs. A typo in a branch that rarely runs can sit there for months.

Rust is compiled. A program called the compiler, rustc, reads all your source first, checks it, and translates it into machine code: the instructions your processor runs directly. The result is a file called a binary (or executable). cargo run is two steps: cargo build calls the compiler and writes the binary to target/debug/snippets, then cargo runs that file. You can run it yourself:

cargo build
./target/debug/snippets

Three things follow from this. Mistakes in types, names and spelling are found before the program ever runs, anywhere in the file, including in branches that rarely run. The binary runs without Rust installed, so you can copy it to another machine of the same kind (here, 64-bit Intel or AMD Linux with a similar system library) and run it there. And nothing changes until you build again: edit the source, forget to rebuild, and the old binary still does the old thing. cargo run always rebuilds what changed, which is why you'll use it most of the time.

The debug in the path is the build profile. A debug build compiles fast and keeps extra checks in. cargo run --release compiles slowly and makes a binary that's often many times faster, written to target/release/. Use debug while you write, and release when you measure speed or ship.

The compiler prints two kinds of message. An error stops the build: there is no new binary until you fix it. A warning doesn't: the program builds and runs, and the compiler is pointing at something that's probably a mistake. The two you'll see most in this page's examples are unused variable (you made a variable and never read it) and field is never read or function is never used, together called dead code. While you're typing examples piece by piece they're expected, because the next piece usually uses the thing. In real work, read each one: a name that starts with _, like _spare, tells the compiler the variable is unused on purpose. Clippy, the linter you'll run before every review, adds warnings of its own.

The shape of a program

// A line that starts with two slashes is a comment.
fn main() {
    let ordered = 12;
    let per_box = 5;
    let boxes = boxes_needed(ordered, per_box);
    println!("{ordered} bolts need {boxes} boxes");
    println!("shipping costs {} cents", shipping_cents(boxes));
}

fn boxes_needed(items: i64, per_box: i64) -> i64 {
    if items == 0 {
        return 0;
    }
    let full = items / per_box;
    if items % per_box == 0 { full } else { full + 1 }
}

fn shipping_cents(boxes: i64) -> i64 {
    899 + boxes * 150
}
12 bolts need 3 boxes
shipping costs 1349 cents
  • Every Rust program starts at a function called main. fn defines a function. The body sits in braces, { }, not under an indent. Indentation is for people; cargo fmt sets it for you.
  • let makes a variable. A line that does something ends with a semicolon.
  • println! prints a line. {ordered} inside the text is replaced by the variable's value, like an f-string.
  • fn boxes_needed(items: i64, per_box: i64) -> i64 is the function's signature: its name, each parameter with its type, and after -> the type it gives back. Every parameter must say its type. There are no default values, no keyword arguments, and no two functions with the same name, so boxes_needed(12, 5) always means one thing.
  • return 0; leaves the function early, as in Python.

The last line of boxes_needed has no semicolon and no return. This is the rule that trips everyone from Python. Rust code is made of statements, which do something and end in ;, and expressions, which produce a value. 899 + boxes * 150 is an expression. So is if ... { full } else { full + 1 }: each branch produces a value, and the if produces whichever branch ran. A block's value is its last expression, if that expression has no semicolon after it. A function's body is a block, so its last expression is what it returns. Add the semicolon and the expression becomes a statement that throws its value away:

fn shipping_cents(boxes: i64) -> i64 {
    899 + boxes * 150;
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", shipping_cents(3));
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:1:34
  |
1 | fn shipping_cents(boxes: i64) -> i64 {
  |    --------------                ^^^ expected `i64`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     899 + boxes * 150;
  |                      - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

() is the empty value, pronounced "unit": what a block gives back when it has nothing to give. Python would return None here and you'd find out three functions later. Rust stops you at the line. return 899 + boxes * 150; would also work, but Rust code leaves the last line bare, and you should too.

Variables, mut and shadowing

const BOX_SIZE: i64 = 5;

fn main() {
    let ordered: i64 = 12;
    let mut shipped = 0;
    shipped += BOX_SIZE;
    shipped += BOX_SIZE;
    println!("shipped {shipped} of {ordered}");

    let sku = "  BRG-6204 ";
    let sku = sku.trim();
    println!("[{sku}]");
}
shipped 10 of 12
[BRG-6204]
  • let ordered: i64 = 12; says the type. Usually you leave it out and the compiler infers it from how the variable is used. Your editor shows inferred types in gray, which is a good way to learn them.
  • Variables can't change unless they're declared let mut. Most values in a program are set once and never change, and when you see mut you know to watch that one. You met the error for this in set up.
  • let sku = sku.trim(); makes a new variable with the same name, which hides the old one. That's shadowing. It's how Rust code says "the cleaned-up version of this from now on" without inventing a name like sku_trimmed.
  • const is a fixed value with a name, written in capitals. Its type is always written out. Put rules like "five to a box" in one, at the top of the file, so the next person can find them.

A type is what kind of value something is, which decides what you can do with it: you can divide numbers and you can trim text, and not the other way round. Python checks types while the program runs, and only on the line that's running. That's called dynamic typing, and it's why "12" + 1 fails in Python only when that line is reached. Rust checks every type of every variable before the program runs, which is static typing. Each variable has exactly one type for its whole life. If you've used pandas, you've met the idea already: every column has a dtype, and int64 and float64 there are i64 and f64 here. Rust gives every variable one.

Numbers have sizes

Python has one integer type that grows as big as it needs to. Rust has several, each with a fixed size, and you choose. The ones you'll use:

TypeWhat it holdsUse it for
i64Whole numbers, about ±9.2 × 1018IDs and amounts from the database. SQLite's integers are this size
i32Whole numbers, about ±2.1 billionWhat a bare 12 becomes if nothing says otherwise
u32, u8Whole numbers that can't be negative, up to about 4.3 billion and up to 255Counts, and bytes
usizeA non-negative whole number the size of a memory address, a byte's position in memory (8 bytes on your machine; under the hood explains)Lengths and positions: .len() returns one, and indexing takes one
f64A floating-point number, Python's float, with the same NaN you know from pandasMeasurements and averages. Not money: ticket 3 shows why
bool, chartrue or false; one character, in single quotesFlags; single letters
 
let quantity: u32 = 40;
let price_cents: i64 = 1_299;
let weight_kg: f64 = 2.5;
let in_stock: bool = true;
let grade: char = 'A';
let line_count: usize = 3;
println!("{quantity} {price_cents} {weight_kg} {in_stock} {grade} {line_count}");
40 1299 2.5 true A 3

The _ in 1_299 is only for your eyes. Dividing two integers gives an integer:

println!("{}", 7 / 2);
println!("{}", -7 / 2);
println!("{}", 7 % 2);
println!("{}", -7 % 2);
println!("{}", 7.0 / 2.0);
3
-3
1
-1
3.5

Integer division drops the fraction, rounding toward zero. Python's // rounds down instead, so -7 // 2 is -4 in Python and -7 / 2 is -3 in Rust. The remainder % follows the same rule, so it keeps the sign of the left side. Only 7.0 / 2.0, with floats on both sides, gives 3.5.

Rust never converts between number types on its own. An f64 total divided by a usize count, which is what every average looks like, doesn't compile:

fn main() {
    let total: f64 = 45.99;
    let count: usize = 4;
    let average = total / count;
    println!("{average}");
}
error[E0277]: cannot divide `f64` by `usize`
 --> src/main.rs:4:25
  |
4 |     let average = total / count;
  |                         ^ no implementation for `f64 / usize`
  |
  = help: the trait `Div<usize>` is not implemented for `f64`
  = help: the following other types implement trait `Div<Rhs>`:
            `&f64` implements `Div<f64>`
            `&f64` implements `Div`
            `f64` implements `Div<&f64>`
            `f64` implements `Div`

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

The help line uses a word you'll see in errors long before ticket 3 teaches it properly. A trait is a named ability that a type can have. Div<usize> is the ability "can be divided by a usize", Display is "can be printed with {}", Ord is "can be put in order". A type implements a trait when it has that ability. So "the trait Div<usize> is not implemented for f64" reads as "an f64 can't be divided by a usize", and the list under it shows what does work: an f64 divided by an f64. Read every "trait X is not implemented for Y" error that way: Y can't do X, so either change the type or use a different operation.

You convert with as:

let total_cents: i64 = 4_599;
let lines: usize = 4;
let average = total_cents as f64 / lines as f64;
println!("{average:.2}");
println!("{}", 3.99_f64 as i64);
println!("{}", 300_i64 as u8);
println!("{}", -1_i64 as u32);
1149.75
3
44
4294967295

as never fails, and that's the danger in it. 3.99 as i64 drops the fraction. 300 as u8 can't fit, so it keeps what fits and gives 44 (under the hood shows why 44). -1 as u32 gives four billion. Use as where nothing can be lost: a whole number into an f64 for an average (exact for any whole number up to about nine quadrillion, far past any count you'll have), or a small count into a bigger type. When a conversion can fail, use one that says so: u8::try_from(x) returns an error for 300 instead of guessing.

Two integer types don't mix either. A u32 quantity times an i64 price is three errors at once, because the compiler can't tell which one you meant to change. Convert the smaller type up to the bigger one before the arithmetic: i64::from(qty) * price, or qty as i64 * price. i64::from only exists for conversions that can't lose anything, which makes it the safer habit.

The ! means macro

println! isn't a function. The ! marks a macro: code that writes code. Before compiling, the compiler expands println!("{ordered} bolts", ...) into the longer code that does the printing. Macros exist for things a function can't do. A Rust function takes a fixed number of arguments of fixed types, and println! takes any number of any type. It also reads your format text while compiling, so a {} with no value to fill it, or a misspelled variable name inside the braces, is a compile error and not a surprise at run time.

A running program has two output channels. Standard output is for its results, and standard error is for messages about how it's going: warnings, errors, debugging. Both appear in your terminal. They separate when you send output somewhere: cargo run > out.txt puts standard output in the file and still shows standard error on screen, so a report file never fills up with complaints.

You'll meet a dozen macros. These are the ones in this course:

MacroWhat it doesFirst used
println!, print!Print to standard output, with and without a line breakHere
eprintln!Print to standard error, where error messages goTicket 6
format!Like println!, but gives you the text as a StringHere
vec!Makes a vector from a list: vec![1, 2, 3]Here
dbg!Prints an expression and its value while you debugHere
writeln!, write!println! and print! into a file, or anything else you can write toTicket 1
matches!Yes or no: does this value fit this pattern?Ticket 3
assert_eq!Stops a test if two values differTicket 4

Formatting output

Rust's format codes are close cousins of Python's f-string codes, so most of what you know carries over:

let sku = "BRG-6204";
let qty = 40;
let price = 12.5;
println!("{sku} x {qty}");
println!("{} boxes of {}", qty / 8, 8);
println!("[{sku:<10}] [{qty:>5}] [{qty:^5}] [{qty:05}]");
println!("[{price:.2}] [{price:>8.2}] [{price:*>8.2}]");
BRG-6204 x 40
5 boxes of 8
[BRG-6204  ] [   40] [ 40  ] [00040]
[12.50] [   12.50] [***12.50]
  • {sku} names a variable. Unlike an f-string, it can only be a plain name, not an expression. For qty / 8, leave the braces empty and put the expressions after the text, in order: "{} boxes of {}", qty / 8, 8.
  • After a colon comes the spec. <10 left-aligns in 10 characters, >5 right-aligns in 5, ^5 centers. 05 pads with zeros. .2 means two decimals, and >8.2 combines them. A character before the alignment, as in *>8.2, is the fill.
  • A doubled brace, {{ or }}, prints a single one.

Plain {} uses a type's display form, meant for people. Numbers and text have one. A list doesn't, because there's no one right way to show a list to a user, so for lists, tuples and your own types you use the debug form, {:?}, meant for programmers:

let line = (sku, qty);
let skus = vec!["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10"];
println!("{line:?}");
println!("{skus:?}");
println!("{skus:#?}");
let label = format!("{qty} units of {sku}");
println!("{label}");
("BRG-6204", 40)
["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10"]
[
    "BRG-6204",
    "BLT-M10",
]
40 units of BRG-6204

{:#?} is the same, spread over lines, which helps for anything big. format! builds the text without printing it.

dbg!, the better print

When something's wrong, you'll want to see values. dbg! prints where it is, the code you wrapped, and the value, then hands the value back, so you can wrap it around a number or a calculation without changing what the program does:

let qty = 40;
let price_cents = 1_299;
let total = dbg!(qty * price_cents);
dbg!(total > 50_000);
println!("total is {total}");
[examples/t0_dbg.rs:8:21] qty * price_cents = 51960
[examples/t0_dbg.rs:9:9] total > 50_000 = true
total is 51960

The first part is the file, line and column. This example lives in examples/; yours will say src/main.rs. dbg! writes to standard error, not standard output, so it stays out of output you send to a file with >. It's for you while you work: take it out before you commit, because a reviewer will ask why it's there. One catch: dbg! takes the value and hands it back, so for something you'll use again, like a String or a Vec, wrap a reference instead: dbg!(&skus).

Choosing and repeating

let qty = 40;
let ships_as = if qty >= 100 {
    "pallet"
} else if qty >= 10 {
    "case"
} else {
    "single"
};
println!("{qty} ships as a {ships_as}");
40 ships as a case

if is an expression, so it can sit on the right of a let, as here. Every branch must produce the same type, and the semicolon goes after the whole thing. No parentheses around the condition. One Python habit doesn't survive: the condition must be a bool. Python's if items: means "if the list isn't empty". Rust has no "truthy" values:

fn main() {
    let skus = vec!["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10"];
    if skus.len() {
        println!("we have {} skus", skus.len());
    }
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:8
  |
3 |     if skus.len() {
  |        ^^^^^^^^^^ expected `bool`, found `usize`

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

Say what you mean: if !skus.is_empty(), or if skus.len() > 1. ! in front of a bool is not.

Loops:

for day in 1..4 {
    print!("{day} ");
}
println!();
for day in 1..=4 {
    print!("{day} ");
}
println!();
for day in (1..=4).rev() {
    print!("{day} ");
}
println!();
for qty in [12, 0, 7, 0, 3] {
    if qty == 0 {
        continue;
    }
    print!("{qty} ");
}
println!();
1 2 3 
1 2 3 4 
4 3 2 1 
12 7 3
  • 1..4 is a range: 1, 2 and 3, the end left out, exactly like Python's range(1, 4). 1..=4 includes the end. .rev() walks it backwards.
  • for works on a range, a list, and anything else that can hand out items one at a time.
  • continue skips to the next item and break leaves the loop, as in Python. print! prints without a line break, and an empty println!() ends the line.
let mut stock = 25;
let mut orders = 0;
while stock >= 8 {
    stock -= 8;
    orders += 1;
}
println!("{orders} orders of 8, {stock} left");

let mut on_hand = 100;
let mut week = 0;
let reorder_week = loop {
    week += 1;
    on_hand -= 30;
    if on_hand < 20 {
        break week;
    }
};
println!("reorder in week {reorder_week}");
3 orders of 8, 1 left
reorder in week 3

while repeats while its condition holds. loop repeats until a break, and break week makes the loop itself produce a value: the week the reorder happens.

A range can also answer "is this number inside?":

let day = 17;
println!("{}", (10..=20).contains(&day));
println!("{}", (10..17).contains(&day));
true
false

If you write day >= 10 && day <= 20, clippy suggests (10..=20).contains(&day) instead. Both are right. Clippy prefers the one where the range is written once. (The & is explained below.) Text works too: ("a".."m").contains(&name).

Tuples, arrays and vectors

let line = ("BRG-6204", 40, 1_299);
let (sku, qty, price) = line;
println!("{sku}: {qty} at {price}");
println!("by position: {} {}", line.0, line.1);

let week: [u32; 5] = [12, 0, 7, 45, 3];
println!("{} days, first {}, last {}", week.len(), week[0], week[4]);

let mut skus = vec!["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10"];
skus.push("HSE-12");
println!("{skus:?}: {} items, empty: {}", skus.len(), skus.is_empty());
BRG-6204: 40 at 1299
by position: BRG-6204 40
5 days, first 12, last 3
["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10", "HSE-12"]: 3 items, empty: false
  • A tuple groups a few values of different types, as in Python. let (sku, qty, price) = line; unpacks it. line.0 is the first item: tuples use a dot and a number, not brackets.
  • An array has a fixed length that's part of its type: [u32; 5] is exactly five u32s. Useful for small fixed lists.
  • A Vec (vector) is Python's list: it grows, and all its items have one type. vec![...] makes one, and push adds to the end, which needs mut.

Reading items:

println!("{:?}", skus.get(1));
println!("{:?}", skus.get(10));
println!("{:?} {:?}", skus.first(), skus.last());
println!("{}", skus[skus.len() - 1]);
Some("BLT-M10")
None
Some("BRG-6204") Some("HSE-12")
HSE-12

skus[0] reads a position, starting from 0. There are no negative positions: Python's skus[-1] is skus[skus.len() - 1], or better, skus.last(). A position past the end doesn't raise an exception for a try block to catch. It stops the program. (Rust has a way to catch a panic, for special cases. It isn't error handling, and this course never uses it.) That's called a panic: the program prints where and why, and stops with exit status 101, a number that tells the shell it failed (under the hood has more).

let qty = vec![12, 0, 7];
let day = 3;
println!("{}", qty[day]);
thread 'main' panicked at examples/t0_panic.rs:10:31:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
exit code: Some(101)

This example ran from the course's examples/ folder, and the exit code line was printed by the program that started it. Yours will name src/main.rs and stop at the note line. One more difference you may hit: when the compiler can see the position is past the end, as with week[7] on the five-item array above, it refuses to build at all, with this operation will panic at runtime. The panic above happens while running because a Vec's length is only known then.

A panic means "the program itself is wrong". When a position might not exist, ask with .get(i), which can't panic. It returns Some(item) when there's an item there and None when there isn't, and first() and last() do the same. That's an Option, coming up shortly.

A slice is a view of a run of items, written with a range:

let qty = vec![12, 0, 7, 45, 3, 18];
println!("{:?}", &qty[1..3]);
println!("{:?}", &qty[..2]);
println!("{:?}", &qty[4..]);
[0, 7]
[12, 0]
[3, 18]
PythonRust
qty[1:3]&qty[1..3]
qty[:2]&qty[..2]
qty[4:]&qty[4..]
qty[-2:]&qty[qty.len() - 2..]

A slice that runs past the end panics, like an index. Python would hand you a shorter list without a word. Walking a list:

for (i, q) in qty.iter().enumerate().take(3) {
    println!("line {i}: {q}");
}
for q in qty.iter().rev().take(2) {
    println!("from the end: {q}");
}
let total: i64 = qty.iter().sum();
println!("total {total}, biggest {:?}, smallest {:?}", qty.iter().max(), qty.iter().min());
line 0: 12
line 1: 0
line 2: 7
from the end: 18
from the end: 3
total 85, biggest Some(45), smallest Some(0)

.iter() makes an iterator: something that hands out the items one at a time. The methods you call on it, such as the ones below, are called iterator methods. .enumerate() pairs each with its position, like Python's enumerate. .take(3) stops after three, and .rev() goes from the end. .sum() adds them up. It can produce several number types, so you name the one you want on the variable: let total: i64. .max() returns an Option, because an empty list has no biggest item. Closures, further down, let you do this on a list of your own structs.

References: & and *

A reference lets code look at a value without taking it. &qty is a reference to qty. Making one is called borrowing. Following a reference to the value it points at is written *:

let qty = vec![12, 0, 7, 45];
let mut big = 0;
for q in &qty {
    if *q > 10 {
        big += 1;
    }
}
println!("{big} big orders out of {}", qty.len());

let first = &qty[0];
println!("first doubled: {}", *first * 2);
2 big orders out of 4
first doubled: 24

for q in &qty borrows the list, so each q is a reference to a number, not the number. Arithmetic works on references to numbers, so first * 2 would also have compiled. Comparison doesn't:

fn main() {
    let qty = vec![12, 0, 7, 45];
    let mut big = 0;
    for q in &qty {
        if q > 10 {
            big += 1;
        }
    }
    println!("{big}");
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:5:16
  |
5 |         if q > 10 {
  |                ^^ expected `&_`, found integer
  |
  = note: expected reference `&_`
                  found type `{integer}`
help: consider dereferencing the borrow
  |
5 |         if *q > 10 {
  |            +

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

The help is right: *q > 10. Now take the & off the loop:

fn main() {
    let skus = vec![String::from("BRG-6204"), String::from("BLT-M10")];
    for sku in skus {
        println!("{sku}");
    }
    println!("{} skus", skus.len());
}
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `skus`
   --> src/main.rs:6:25
    |
2   |     let skus = vec![String::from("BRG-6204"), String::from("BLT-M10")];
    |         ---- move occurs because `skus` has type `Vec<String>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
3   |     for sku in skus {
    |                ---- `skus` moved due to this implicit call to `.into_iter()`
...
6   |     println!("{} skus", skus.len());
    |                         ^^^^ value borrowed here after move
    |
note: `into_iter` takes ownership of the receiver `self`, which moves `skus`
   --> ~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/core/src/iter/traits/collect.rs:310:18
    |
310 |     fn into_iter(self) -> Self::IntoIter;
    |                  ^^^^
help: consider iterating over a slice of the `Vec<String>`'s content to avoid moving into the `for` loop
    |
3   |     for sku in &skus {
    |                +

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

Without the &, the loop takes the vector itself and uses it up, so it's gone afterward. That's called a move. Python never does this, and it's the idea at the center of Rust, which ticket 1 explains properly. For now: loop over &list unless you're finished with the list.

Some values don't move, because copying them is as cheap as moving them. Numbers, bool, char and &str are like that, and so is an array made only of them. Those types are called Copy: using one by value hands over a copy and leaves the original usable. So for q in qty over an array of numbers leaves qty usable after the loop. A Vec is never Copy, even a Vec of numbers, because it owns a block of memory stored elsewhere, so the loop in the error above moved it. A String is the same.

Structs and methods

A struct is a named group of fields, each with a type. It's the shape of one row of a DataFrame, with the column types written down, or a @dataclass if you've used one. An impl block ("implementation") holds the functions that belong to it:

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Bin {
    location: String,
    capacity: u32,
    on_hand: u32,
}

impl Bin {
    fn new(location: &str, capacity: u32) -> Self {
        Bin {
            location: location.to_string(),
            capacity,
            on_hand: 0,
        }
    }

    fn space_left(&self) -> u32 {
        self.capacity - self.on_hand
    }

    fn put_away(&mut self, qty: u32) -> u32 {
        let stored = qty.min(self.space_left());
        self.on_hand += stored;
        stored
    }
}
let mut bin = Bin::new("A-04-2", 50);
let stored = bin.put_away(30);
println!("{}: stored {stored}, {} left", bin.location, bin.space_left());
let stored = bin.put_away(30);
println!("stored {stored}, {} left", bin.space_left());
println!("{bin:?}");
A-04-2: stored 30, 20 left
stored 20, 0 left
Bin { location: "A-04-2", capacity: 50, on_hand: 50 }
  • Self means "the type this impl is for", here Bin. new is a plain function that builds one. Rust has no constructors and no __init__; new is only a naming habit, and everyone follows it.
  • location: &str takes borrowed text, and .to_string() makes the bin its own copy, a String, to keep. Text, briefly explains the two text types.
  • In Bin { location: ..., capacity, on_hand: 0 }, a bare capacity is short for capacity: capacity.
  • A function whose first parameter is some form of self is a method. &self borrows the bin to read it. &mut self borrows it to change it. Python's self is always the second kind; Rust makes you say which, so the signature tells you whether a call can change the value. That's why bin must be let mut: put_away takes &mut self.
  • Bin::new(...) uses ::, because new belongs to the type and there's no bin yet. bin.put_away(30) uses a dot, because it's called on a value. In general :: walks into a type or a module (a named group of code, below), and . reaches into a value.
  • qty.min(...) is a method too, on u32. Numbers have dozens.
  • #[derive(Debug)] asks the compiler to write the code that makes {:?} work for Bin. Ticket 3 explains what else derive can write.

Maybe a value, maybe an error: Option and Result

Rust has no None that can turn up anywhere and no exceptions. Two types take their place, and you'll handle one of them on nearly every line of real code.

Option<T> is "maybe a T": either Some(value) or None. The <T> is a type parameter: Option<u32> is maybe a u32, Option<&str> is maybe some text. Vec<T> works the same way, which is why a list of SKUs is a Vec<&str>. You find out which one you have with match:

let skus = ["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10"];
match skus.get(5) {
    Some(sku) => println!("found {sku}"),
    None => println!("nothing at position 5"),
}
if let Some(sku) = skus.first() {
    println!("the first is {sku}");
}
nothing at position 5
the first is BRG-6204

match lists the shapes a value can have, each followed by => and what to do. Some(sku) matches a value and names what's inside. The compiler checks that you covered every shape, so you can't forget None. if let Some(sku) = ... is a match for when you only care about one shape.

Result<T, E> is "a T, or an error of type E": Ok(value) or Err(error). Anything that can fail returns one, such as turning text into a number:

for raw in ["40", "forty", " 40"] {
    match raw.parse::<u32>() {
        Ok(qty) => println!("{raw:?} is {qty}"),
        Err(e) => println!("{raw:?} is no good: {e}"),
    }
}
let per_case: u32 = "12".parse().expect("I typed this number myself");
println!("{per_case} per case");
"40" is 40
"forty" is no good: invalid digit found in string
" 40" is no good: invalid digit found in string
12 per case
  • raw.parse::<u32>() says which type to parse into. The ::<u32> is nicknamed the turbofish. You can write the type on the variable instead, as the per_case line does: let per_case: u32 = ...parse().
  • " 40" fails. parse doesn't trim spaces for you, unlike Python's int(" 40").
  • .expect("...") means "give me the value, and if it's an error, panic with this message". It's there for things that can't fail, and the message should say why.

.unwrap() is expect without the message. You'll see it everywhere in examples online. Here's what it does with bad data:

let qty: u32 = "forty".parse().unwrap();
thread 'main' panicked at examples/t0_panic.rs:16:44:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
exit code: Some(101)

That's why the tickets ban it on anything that came from outside the program. A month-end run that panics on one mistyped row has lost every row after it. Bad data is a Result to handle, and a panic is for bugs. Ticket 1 shows ?, the short way to pass an error up to the caller.

Closures: doing something to every item

A Vec of your own structs is the Rust shape of a DataFrame: one struct per row. Picking a column, or the row with the biggest value, takes a small function that says what to look at:

struct Item {
    sku: String,
    qty: u32,
}

fn main() {
    let items = vec![
        Item {
            sku: "BRG-6204".to_string(),
            qty: 40,
        },
        Item {
            sku: "BLT-M10".to_string(),
            qty: 500,
        },
        Item {
            sku: "HSE-12".to_string(),
            qty: 12,
        },
    ];

    let total: u32 = items.iter().map(|item| item.qty).sum();
    println!("{total} units");

    if let Some(item) = items.iter().max_by_key(|item| item.qty) {
        println!("most: {} ({})", item.sku, item.qty);
    }

    let mut few = Vec::new();
    for item in &items {
        if item.qty < 100 {
            few.push(&item.sku);
        }
    }
    println!("under 100: {few:?}");
}
552 units
most: BLT-M10 (500)
under 100: ["BRG-6204", "HSE-12"]
  • |item| item.qty is a closure: a function with no name, written where it's used. The parameters go between the bars and the body follows. Python's lambda item: item.qty is the same idea.
  • .map(...) runs the closure on each item and hands out the results, so .map(|item| item.qty) is the quantity column. .sum() adds it up.
  • .max_by_key(...) returns the item whose closure value is biggest, as an Option, because an empty list has none. On a tie it returns the last of the tied items.
  • Vec::new() makes an empty vector. The compiler works out what it holds from what you push, here &String, references to each item's SKU.

That's enough to use them this week. Ticket 1 explains closures properly, along with filter, count and the rest.

Text, briefly

let literal = "Carriage bolt";
let owned: String = literal.to_string();
let size = String::from("M10");
let label = format!("{owned} {size}");
println!("{label}, {} bytes", label.len());
Carriage bolt M10, 17 bytes

Rust has two text types, and the difference matters from ticket 1 on. Text in quotes in your source is a &str: a borrowed view of text stored somewhere else, here inside the program file. String is text the variable owns and can grow. .to_string() and String::from make a String from a &str, and format! builds a new one. .len() counts bytes, not letters, and under the hood explains why those differ. Tickets 1 and 2 explain when to use which type.

Imports and the prelude

fn main() {
    let mut stock = HashMap::new();
    stock.insert("BRG-6204", 40);
    println!("{stock:?}");
}
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared type `HashMap`
 --> src/main.rs:2:21
  |
2 |     let mut stock = HashMap::new();
  |                     ^^^^^^^ use of undeclared type `HashMap`
  |
help: consider importing this struct
  |
1 + use std::collections::HashMap;
  |

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0433`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

std is the standard library, the code that comes with Rust. std::collections::HashMap is a path: the HashMap type, in the collections module, in std. A module is a named group of code, like a Python module. use std::collections::HashMap; at the top of the file lets you write HashMap alone, like Python's from collections import Counter.

A few names need no use, because they're in the prelude, a short list Rust imports into every file: Vec, String, Option, Some, None, Result, Ok, Err and a handful of others. Everything else needs one. When the compiler says "consider importing", it's almost always right.

Reading the docs

You will spend more time in the documentation than in any book. The standard library's is at doc.rust-lang.org/std, and rustup doc --std opens a copy offline. Every published crate has its docs at docs.rs, and cargo doc --open builds the docs for your project and every crate it uses. Your editor's hover shows the same text for whatever is under the cursor.

On a type's page, such as Vec, the search box at the top finds anything by name. Below the description are the type's methods, then "Trait Implementations", which lists the things the type can do through traits. Ticket 3 shows how to give your own types traits. A method you can't find among the methods is often in there. A Vec also has every method of a slice, listed under "Methods from Deref<Target = [T]>": that's where first, last and get live. Each method starts with its signature, and reading one is a skill worth practicing:

  • pub fn push(&mut self, value: T) on Vec. pub means anyone can call it. &mut self means it changes the vector, so your variable needs mut. It takes one item of the vector's item type, T, and there's no ->, so it returns nothing. You know all that before reading a word of the description.
  • pub fn trim(&self) -> &str on str. It only reads the text, and it returns a borrowed view, so it doesn't copy anything.
  • pub fn split_once<P>(&self, delimiter: P) -> Option<(&str, &str)> on str, followed by where P: Pattern. Together those say the delimiter can be any type that can be searched for, such as a char or a &str. It returns maybe a pair of borrowed pieces: None when the delimiter isn't there.

Some signatures look worse than they are. get's is full of angle brackets because it accepts a range as well as a position. On a first read, skip what's inside the angle brackets and read the rest. One more piece of syntax you'll see in signatures and examples: _ means "something I'm not naming". In a match, _ => matches anything left over. let _ = ...; throws a value away on purpose. Vec<_> means "a vector of whatever the compiler works out". The symbol lookup at the end of this page lists every piece of punctuation in the course, for when you meet one and can't remember it.

When the compiler's help is wrong

The help line is right most of the time. It's a suggestion for making the code compile, though, not for making it correct, and a few suggestions compile while doing the wrong thing. Before you take one, check it against what you know. The ones in this course:

  • (total / count) as f64. It divides as integers first, dropping the fraction, then converts. Convert each side: total as f64 / count as f64.
  • (qty * price).into() for a u32 times an i64. The multiplication is what fails, so converting its result can't help. Convert qty before multiplying.
  • .to_string() when you compare a String with a &str. It compiles by copying the text every time. Compare my_string.as_str() with the &str instead. Ticket 1 explains why that works.
  • "consider removing the borrow". Taking the & off often turns a type error into a move error a moment later. When it does, the & was right and something else needs to change.
  • .clone(), suggested to get past a move or borrow error. It works by copying, and it hides the question the error was asking: who should own this value? Ticket 1 is about answering it.

Warm-up drills

Put drills in a program of their own. Cargo treats every file in src/bin/ as a separate program named after the file, so make src/bin/drills.rs with its own main and run it with cargo run --bin drills. Once there's more than one program, plain cargo run stops and asks which one you mean. Keep it running src/main.rs by adding default-run = "snippets" under [package] in Cargo.toml, the project's settings file. [package] starts a section, and each line under it is a setting. After the edit, the whole file is:

[package]
name = "snippets"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
default-run = "snippets"

[dependencies]

Give each drill its own function (fn drill_1() and so on) and call them from main, so drills don't share variables. A compile error anywhere in the file still stops the whole program from building, so undo each break-it mistake as soon as you've read its error.

Drill 1. Eight days of orders for one part: let qty = [12, 0, 7, 45, 3, 18, 0, 22];. With one for loop and no iterator methods, print how many days there are, how many had orders, the total, the biggest day, and the average over the days that had orders, with two decimals.

8 days, 6 with orders
107 units, biggest day 45
average 17.83 units per ordering day

Drill 2. let skus = ["BRG-6204", "BLT-M10", "HSE-12", "BRG-6305", "GKT-8"];. Print the position and SKU of every bearing (the ones starting BRG), then the last two SKUs as a slice, then how many bytes the first one has. You need a str method that checks how text starts: find it on the str page and read its signature before you use it.

0: BRG-6204
3: BRG-6305
last two: ["BRG-6305", "GKT-8"]
first has 8 bytes

Drill 3. Prices are whole cents: let prices = [("BRG-6204", 1_299), ("BLT-M10", 18), ("GKT-8", 205), ("CHN-40", 12_995)];. Print a price list with the SKU left-aligned in 10 characters, then the dollars right-aligned in 5, a dot and the cents, without any f64. Integer division and the remainder give you the two halves. Print the cents with a plain {} first, look at what happens to 205, then fix it with a format spec from above.

BRG-6204     12.99
BLT-M10       0.18
GKT-8         2.05
CHN-40      129.95

Drill 4: break it. One at a time, make each of these mistakes in a drill, read the whole error, and undo it. Put a semicolon after a function's last line. Remove a mut. Make a vec! of Strings, loop over it without & and use it after the loop. Read skus[10] on drill 2's array, then on a vec! with the same SKUs, then skus.get(10). Write let first = skus[0][0]; to get the first letter of a SKU. Divide an integer total by skus.len() into an f64, and check the compiler's suggestion against the list above. In your journal, write one line per mistake: did it fail when compiling or when running, and what did the message tell you to do?

This one isn't from Dana: it's the exercise at the end of the wiki page, and everyone writes it. Make src/bin/week0.rs in your snippets project. It holds five order lines, written into the code:

SKUQuantityUnit price (cents)
BRG-6204411299
BLT-M1050018
HSE-12124550

Before you type, answer these in your journal. What type is each field, and why? Which of the summary numbers need the list of lines walked once, and can one loop compute several of them? Stuck?

Hint 1: where the data lives

Build the five lines in main with your new function, inside vec![...] or an array. A method like fn line_cents(&self) -> i64 keeps the multiplication in one place, so the table, the total and the average all agree.

Hint 2: printing cents as dollars

53259 cents is 53259 / 100 dollars and 53259 % 100 cents. Print the cents with a spec that pads to two digits with zeros, or 90 dollars prints as 90.0. To make the dollars-and-cents pair fill a 10-character column, give the dollars part a width of 7: seven, plus the dot, plus two.

Hint 3: the biggest line

Keep a reference to the best line so far, starting with the first one, and replace it inside the loop when a line beats it. &lines[0] is safe here because you wrote five lines into the code yourself. Or use .iter().max_by_key(...) from closures, which keeps the whole line, SKU included, and handle the Option it returns with match or if let. Check what each way does on a tie.

Under the hood

Don't skip this one. Every later ticket assumes it.

Bits, bytes and integers

A computer stores everything as bits, each 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte. A u8 is one byte read as a number in base 2: each bit is worth twice the one to its right, so 00000101 is 4 + 1 = 5. Eight bits have 256 patterns, so a u8 holds 0 to 255. A u32 is four bytes and an i64 is eight.

println!("{:>4} = {:08b}", 5u8, 5u8);
println!("{:>4} = {:08b}", 200u8, 200u8);
println!("{:>4} = {:08b}", -1i8, -1i8);
println!("{:>4} = {:08b}", -128i8, -128i8);
println!("u8  {} to {}", u8::MIN, u8::MAX);
println!("i8  {} to {}", i8::MIN, i8::MAX);
println!("i64 {} to {}", i64::MIN, i64::MAX);
   5 = 00000101
 200 = 11001000
  -1 = 11111111
-128 = 10000000
u8  0 to 255
i8  -128 to 127
i64 -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807

Signed types like i8 use two's complement. The leftmost bit counts as minus its usual value, so in an i8 it's worth −128 instead of 128. All eight bits set is −128 + 127 = −1, and a lone left bit is −128. The payoff is that the processor adds signed and unsigned numbers with the same circuit. It also explains -1 as u32 above: as keeps the bits and changes how they're read, and all ones read as unsigned is the largest u32. 300 as u8 keeps only the lowest eight bits of 300, which is 300 − 256 = 44.

A fixed size means a sum can be too big to fit. That's overflow, and Rust gives you methods to choose what happens:

let stock: u8 = 250;
println!("{:?}", stock.checked_add(5));
println!("{:?}", stock.checked_add(10));
println!("{}", stock.wrapping_add(10));
println!("{}", stock.saturating_add(10));
Some(255)
None
4
255

checked_add returns None when the result doesn't fit. wrapping_add goes round like a car's odometer: 250 + 10 is 260, minus 256 is 4. saturating_add stops at the maximum. A plain + that overflows panics in a debug build:

let stock: u8 = std::hint::black_box(250);
let more = stock + 10;
println!("{more}");
thread 'main' panicked at examples/t0_panic.rs:24:24:
attempt to add with overflow
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
exit code: Some(101)

Built with --release, the same lines don't panic: the addition wraps, and it prints 4. That's a choice made for speed, and it's why code that adds up numbers from outside the program uses checked_add. (black_box only stops the compiler from noticing the overflow while compiling, which it otherwise would.) Python never overflows because its integers grow, and pays for that with speed and memory on every operation.

Memory is a long row of numbered bytes

While your program runs, its data lives in memory, which you can picture as one very long row of bytes, each with a number called its address. A variable is a name for a few bytes in that row. How many depends on the type:

use std::mem::size_of;
println!("u8    {} byte", size_of::<u8>());
println!("bool  {} byte", size_of::<bool>());
println!("i32   {} bytes", size_of::<i32>());
println!("u32   {} bytes", size_of::<u32>());
println!("char  {} bytes", size_of::<char>());
println!("i64   {} bytes", size_of::<i64>());
println!("f64   {} bytes", size_of::<f64>());
println!("usize {} bytes", size_of::<usize>());
println!("&i64  {} bytes", size_of::<&i64>());
u8    1 byte
bool  1 byte
i32   4 bytes
u32   4 bytes
char  4 bytes
i64   8 bytes
f64   8 bytes
usize 8 bytes
&i64  8 bytes

A char takes four bytes because it can hold any single Unicode scalar value. Unicode gives every symbol in every writing system a number, a code point, and a scalar value is any code point outside a small reserved range. A reference such as &i64 is an address: eight bytes on a 64-bit machine, whatever it points at. That's also why usize is eight bytes here: it's defined as the size of an address, so it can count as far as memory goes. The addresses themselves change every run, because the operating system shuffles where a program's memory starts, as a defense against attacks. Ticket 1 shows where a Vec and a String keep their contents.

A value that holds an address is called a pointer, and a reference is a pointer with rules. Rust checks that every reference points at a live value. There is no null reference, the "points at nothing" value that crashes C and Java programs: where something might be missing, Rust uses Option, and the compiler makes you check.

Getting memory for a value is allocating it, and handing it back when you're done is freeing it. In C you free by hand, and freeing too early or twice is a classic crash. Python has a garbage collector, a part of the running program that finds values nothing uses anymore and frees them. Rust has neither. Every value has one owner, usually a variable, and when the owner's block ends at its closing brace, its scope ends and the value is dropped: freed, right there. That's the rule behind every borrow error you'll meet: a reference can't outlive the value it points at.

Text is bytes

Text is stored as numbers too. ASCII, from the 1960s, numbers 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation), each fitting in one byte. Unicode numbers every character in every script, about 150,000 so far. Each one's number is its code point. UTF-8 is the standard way to store code points as bytes: ASCII characters take one byte, as before, and everything else takes two to four. Rust's text is always UTF-8.

for word in ["M10", "Ø25mm", "5µm", "café"] {
    println!("{word:<6} {} bytes, {} chars", word.len(), word.chars().count());
}
println!("{:?}", "café".as_bytes());
println!("{:?}", "café".chars().next());
println!("{}", &"BRG-6204"[..3]);
M10    3 bytes, 3 chars
Ø25mm  6 bytes, 5 chars
5µm    4 bytes, 3 chars
café   5 bytes, 4 chars
[99, 97, 102, 195, 169]
Some('c')
BRG

é is two bytes, 195 and 169, so café is four characters and five bytes. Python's len("café") is 4 because Python counts code points. Rust's .len() counts bytes, because that's what the computer stores and what it costs to copy, and .chars().count() counts chars, which are code points. (Those usually match what you'd call characters. Not always: an accent can be stored as its own code point after the letter, and some emoji are several joined together.) Since characters have different widths, finding the fifth one means reading from the start, so Rust won't let you write sku[0]:

fn main() {
    let sku = "BRG-6204";
    let first = sku[0];
    println!("{first}");
}
error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`
 --> src/main.rs:3:21
  |
3 |     let first = sku[0];
  |                     ^ string indices are ranges of `usize`
  |
  = help: the trait `SliceIndex<str>` is not implemented for `{integer}`
  = note: you can use `.chars().nth()` or `.bytes().nth()`
          for more information, see chapter 8 in The Book: <https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch08-02-strings.html#indexing-into-strings>
  = help: the following other types implement trait `SliceIndex<T>`:
            `usize` implements `SliceIndex<ByteStr>`
            `usize` implements `SliceIndex<[T]>`
  = note: required for `str` to implement `Index<{integer}>`

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

.chars().next() gets the first character. &sku[..3] is a slice by byte position, which is fine for ASCII codes like SKUs and panics if the position falls in the middle of a character. Hand-typed data is full of characters you didn't expect, as ticket 4 finds out.

Your program is a process

A running program is a process. The operating system gives each one its own memory, the arguments it was started with, and a current working directory: the folder it counts as "here". A relative path like data/kettle_creek.db is looked up from that folder, not from where the source file is:

use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::path::Path;

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    fs::create_dir_all("orders")?;
    fs::write("orders/today.txt", "BRG-6204,40\n")?;
    let today = Path::new("orders/today.txt");
    println!("from here:   {}", today.exists());
    env::set_current_dir("orders")?;
    println!("from orders: {}", today.exists());
    Ok(())
}
from here:   true
from orders: false

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> lets main fail with a file-system error, and the ? after each call means "if this failed, stop here and pass the error on". Ticket 1 explains both. The program makes a folder with a file in it, then moves into the folder. The same relative path that found the file a moment ago finds nothing, because "here" changed. cargo run runs your program from wherever you typed it, so run it from the project folder, where data/ is. In Python the same thing happens, and it's why a notebook that works stops working when you move it.

When a process ends, it hands back one number, its exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure. A panic exits with 101, as you saw above. Your shell keeps the last one:

cargo run --bin week0
echo $?

Schedulers and scripts read that number to decide whether your program worked. Ticket 6 makes your program set it on purpose.

Go deeper

  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 1, then chapter 3: Common Programming Concepts, which covers this page's first half in more depth. Chapter 2 is a small game that uses most of it at once.
  • Chapter 5.3: Method Syntax, for impl, self and associated functions.
  • Rust by Example: Formatted print and Primitives: short runnable examples, one feature each.
  • The std::fmt docs, the full format mini-language. Keep it bookmarked.
  • Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software by Charles Petzold, 2nd edition (2022). How a computer works, built up from a flashlight to a processor, for people with no background at all. It's written for exactly the reader of this page's "under the hood".
  • Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective by Bryant and O'Hallaron, chapter 2, "Representing and Manipulating Information": bits, integers, two's complement and floating point, properly. A university textbook, and the one ticket 1 points at too.
  • Joel Spolsky, "The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets" (2003), and UTF-8 Everywhere, for why UTF-8 won.
