This ticket teaches structs, Vec, iterators and closures, borrowing, Result and ?, sorting and writing a file. Under the hood: the stack and the heap, and why ISO dates sort as text. Crates allowed: rusqlite.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Reading the database

From a table to a Vec

Every program in Part 1 has the same three steps: load rows into Rust values, work on them in Rust, write the result. This page covers all three. The examples use a tiny lending library rather than our own tables, so you can try things without touching real data. The shapes carry straight over.

The practice library database

The examples import it as snippets::library, from the snippets scratch project you made in week zero. Add rusqlite to it. (If you set default-run in week zero, plain cargo run still runs src/main.rs.)

cd ~/projects/snippets
cargo add rusqlite --features bundled

Save the code below as src/lib.rs, beside src/main.rs. A package can hold a library and a program at once, and the program reaches the library by the package's name, so use snippets::library; at the top of src/main.rs brings the function in. (Ticket 5 explains libraries properly.) Then type an example into src/main.rs and cargo run. The database is built in memory each run, so nothing is saved.

use rusqlite::{Connection, Result};

/// A tiny lending library, built in memory, for trying things out.
pub fn library() -> Result<Connection> {
    let db = Connection::open_in_memory()?;
    db.execute_batch(
        "CREATE TABLE books (
             book_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
             title   TEXT NOT NULL,
             author  TEXT NOT NULL
         );
         CREATE TABLE loans (
             loan_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
             book_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
             member      TEXT NOT NULL,
             loaned_on   TEXT NOT NULL,
             returned_on TEXT,
             status      TEXT NOT NULL
         );
         CREATE TABLE fines (
             loan_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
             amount  REAL NOT NULL
         );
         INSERT INTO books VALUES
             (101, 'The Mythical Man-Month', 'Brooks'),
             (102, 'Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs', 'Abelson'),
             (103, 'The Art of Computer Programming', 'Knuth'),
             (104, 'A Discipline of Programming', 'Dijkstra'),
             (105, 'Notes on the Synthesis of Form', 'Alexander');
         INSERT INTO loans VALUES
             (1, 101, 'Ada',    '2026-08-03', '2026-08-20', 'returned'),
             (2, 102, 'Grace',  '2026-08-11', NULL,         'out'),
             (3, 103, 'Alan',   '2026-09-01', NULL,         'out'),
             (4, 101, 'Grace',  '2026-09-02', '2026-09-15', 'returned'),
             (5, 104, 'Edsger', '2026-09-28', NULL,         'out'),
             (6, 105, 'Ada',    '2026-07-19', NULL,         'lost'),
             (7, 103, 'Grace',  '2026-07-30', '2026-08-29', 'returned');
         INSERT INTO fines VALUES
             (1, 0.10), (1, 0.20), (4, 0.30), (6, 24.95), (7, 0.70), (7, 0.10);",
    )?;
    Ok(db)
}

Three things in it are new. /// starts a doc comment, which describes the item below it; your editor shows it when you hover over the name. use rusqlite::{Connection, Result}; imports two names from one crate at once: the braces hold a list. And this Result is rusqlite's own. It's a type alias, a short name for a longer type: rusqlite::Result<T> means Result<T, rusqlite::Error>. It's week zero's two-part Result with the error type already filled in.

Describe a row with a struct

A struct is a named group of fields, each with a type. Think of one row of a table with its column types written down. A Vec of them plays the part of a DataFrame's rows. (If you've met Python's @dataclass, a struct is that, except the types are checked when the program is compiled.)

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
    loaned_on: String,
    returned_on: Option<String>,
    status: String,
}

Pick each field's type from the column:

  • INTEGER becomes i64, a 64-bit signed integer. SQLite's integers are 64-bit, so i64 always fits.
  • TEXT becomes String: text that the struct owns. You'll see its cousin &str in a moment.
  • A column that can be NULL becomes Option<T>. Option<String> is either Some(text) or None. Rust has no null, so a missing value has to be visible in the type, and the compiler makes you handle it before you use it.

#[derive(Debug)] asks the compiler to write the code that prints the struct with {:?}. Making one and printing it:

let loan = Loan {
    loan_id: 2,
    member: String::from("Grace"),
    loaned_on: "2026-08-11".to_string(),
    returned_on: None,
    status: "out".to_string(),
};
println!("{} borrowed on {}", loan.member, loan.loaned_on);
println!("{:?}", loan);
println!("{loan:#?}");
Grace borrowed on 2026-08-11
Loan { loan_id: 2, member: "Grace", loaned_on: "2026-08-11", returned_on: None, status: "out" }
Loan {
    loan_id: 2,
    member: "Grace",
    loaned_on: "2026-08-11",
    returned_on: None,
    status: "out",
}

"2026-08-11" on its own is a &str, a borrowed view of text that's baked into the program. A struct field of type String needs text it owns, so .to_string() or String::from(...) makes an owned copy. {:#?} is the pretty, multi-line form of {:?}.

Load the rows

Here is the whole load step, with main:

use rusqlite::Connection;
use snippets::library;
use std::error::Error;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
    loaned_on: String,
    returned_on: Option<String>,
    status: String,
}

fn load_loans(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>> {
    let mut stmt =
        db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, member, loaned_on, returned_on, status FROM loans")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |row| {
        Ok(Loan {
            loan_id: row.get(0)?,
            member: row.get(1)?,
            loaned_on: row.get(2)?,
            returned_on: row.get(3)?,
            status: row.get(4)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let db = library()?;
    let loans = load_loans(&db)?;
    println!("loaded {} loans", loans.len());
    for loan in &loans {
        println!(
            "{} {:<6} {} {:?} {}",
            loan.loan_id, loan.member, loan.loaned_on, loan.returned_on, loan.status
        );
    }
    Ok(())
}
loaded 7 loans
1 Ada    2026-08-03 Some("2026-08-20") returned
2 Grace  2026-08-11 None out
3 Alan   2026-09-01 None out
4 Grace  2026-09-02 Some("2026-09-15") returned
5 Edsger 2026-09-28 None out
6 Ada    2026-07-19 None lost
7 Grace  2026-07-30 Some("2026-08-29") returned

Line by line:

  • db.prepare(...) compiles the SQL once and gives back a statement. It can fail (a typo in the SQL, say), so it returns a Result, and the ? passes any error up to the caller.
  • stmt.query_map([], |row| ...) runs the query and calls the closure |row| ... once per row. A closure is an inline function, like Python's lambda but allowed to be as long as you like. The [] means "no parameters".
  • The closure ends in Ok(Loan { ... }) because query_map wants each row's answer as a Result: a loan, or the error that stopped it. A ? inside a closure returns from the closure, not from load_loans. It ends that one row's call with the error, and query_map passes the error on.
  • row.get(0)? reads column 0 and converts it to whatever type the field needs. The compiler works out the type from the struct field. If the conversion fails, for example a NULL going into a String, you get an error, not a silent empty string.
  • rows.collect() runs through every row and gathers the results. The function's return type, rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>>, tells collect what to build: either every row in a Vec, or the first error.
  • fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> lets main use ? too. On success it returns Ok(()), where () is Rust's "nothing". On failure it returns an error, and Rust prints it and exits with a failure code. For now, read Box<dyn Error> as "any kind of error". Ticket 6 explains what dyn means, and ticket 5 replaces it with an error type of your own. For a program this size, it is enough error handling.

From here on, most examples are pieces of main. They use ?, so type them into a main that returns Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>, like the one above, with use std::error::Error; at the top of the file. Forget the return type and you get one of the most common errors there is:

fn main() {
    let count: i64 = "42".parse()?;
    println!("{count}");
}
error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another type that implements `FromResidual`)
 --> src/main.rs:2:34
  |
1 | fn main() {
  | --------- this function should return `Result` or `Option` to accept `?`
2 |     let count: i64 = "42".parse()?;
  |                                  ^ cannot use the `?` operator in a function that returns `()`
  |
help: consider adding return type
  |
1 ~ fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
2 |     let count: i64 = "42".parse()?;
3 |     println!("{count}");
4 +     Ok(())
  |

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.

Your own database file

The examples use library(). Your program opens the real file instead, by a path relative to the folder you run cargo run from. Your snippets project has no database yet, so copy one in before you try this:

cd ~/projects/snippets
mkdir -p data
cp ~/projects/kettle_creek/data/kettle_creek.db data/
use rusqlite::Connection;

let db = Connection::open("data/kettle_creek.db")?;
let n: i64 = db.query_row("SELECT count(*) FROM suppliers", [], |row| row.get(0))?;
println!("{n} suppliers");
24 suppliers

(query_row is for a query that returns exactly one row. It's here to keep the example short. Your loaders use query_map.) The path is relative, so it's looked up from the folder the program runs in. cargo run from the project folder finds data/kettle_creek.db. Run it from src/ and it won't. Week zero's under the hood has more on the working directory.

One trap: Connection::open creates an empty database if the file doesn't exist, so a typo in the path doesn't fail where you made it. It fails later, and confusingly:

let db = Connection::open("data_kettle_creek.db")?; // typo: _ for /
let result = db.prepare("SELECT supplier_id, name FROM suppliers");
println!("{:?}", result.err().map(|e| e.to_string()));
Some("no such table: suppliers")

If you typed that in, it also left an empty file called data_kettle_creek.db in your project folder. Delete it (rm data_kettle_creek.db) so it doesn't end up in a commit. Opening read-only refuses a missing file at once, with the path in the message, and it guarantees your program can't change the warehouse data:

use rusqlite::OpenFlags;

let flags = OpenFlags::SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY;
let result = Connection::open_with_flags("data/kettle-creek.db", flags); // typo: - for _
println!("{:?}", result.err().map(|e| e.to_string()));
Some("unable to open database file: data/kettle-creek.db")

In Python you'd write rows = cursor.execute(sql).fetchall() and get a list of tuples. Here you get a Vec of structs whose fields have names and types. That costs you the struct definition, and pays you back every time you type loan. and your editor lists the fields.

Work on the rows

A Vec<T> is Rust's growable list, the equivalent of a Python list whose items all have one type. To count loans that are out:

fn count_out(loans: &[Loan]) -> usize {
    loans.iter().filter(|loan| loan.status == "out").count()
}

.iter() walks the items one at a time without changing or consuming them. .filter(...) keeps the items its closure says yes to, and .count() counts them. Nothing runs until count asks for items. These chains are called iterator adaptors, and they're how most Rust code works through collections. The same thing as a loop:

fn count_out(loans: &[Loan]) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for loan in loans {
        if loan.status == "out" {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

Both compile to essentially the same machine code. Use whichever reads better. Here the chain does: it says "count the out loans" in one line. In Python the chain is sum(1 for loan in loans if loan.status == "out"), and in pandas it's (df.status == "out").sum(). filter does the job of a boolean mask.

Closures can do more than |x| x + 1. Four things you'll see from here on:

// A closure can use variables from around it. This one uses `fine_per_day`.
let fine_per_day = 25;
let days_late = [0, 3, 12];
let fines: Vec<i64> = days_late.iter().map(|days| days * fine_per_day).collect();
println!("fines in cents: {fines:?}");

// `|_|` takes an argument and ignores it.
let parsed: Result<i64, &str> = "12x".parse::<i64>().map_err(|_| "not a number");
println!("{parsed:?}");

// A function's name is a value too: `String::from` is passed, not called.
let returned_on: Option<&str> = Some("2026-08-20");
let owned: Option<String> = returned_on.map(String::from);
println!("{owned:?}");

// `||` takes no arguments. This one only runs if there's no member.
let member: Option<&str> = None;
let shown = member
    .map(String::from)
    .unwrap_or_else(|| format!("nobody, fined {fine_per_day}c a day"));
println!("{shown}");
fines in cents: [0, 75, 300]
Err("not a number")
Some("2026-08-20")
nobody, fined 25c a day
  • A closure can use the variables around it. This is called capturing. fine_per_day isn't a parameter, but the closure can read it.
  • |_| takes an argument and ignores it. || takes no arguments at all. unwrap_or_else(|| ...) calls its closure only when there's no value, so the format! doesn't run when it isn't needed.
  • The name of a function is a value you can hand over, without the parentheses. .map(String::from) is the same as .map(|s| String::from(s)).

Borrowing, in five minutes

Look at the parameter: loans: &[Loan], not loans: Vec<Loan>. The & means count_out borrows the loans: it can read them, and the caller still has them afterward. This is the idea that makes Rust Rust, so here is what happens without it:

fn total_len(names: Vec<String>) -> usize {
    names.iter().map(|n| n.len()).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Grace")];
    let n = total_len(names);
    println!("{n} letters across {} names", names.len());
}
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `names`
 --> src/main.rs:8:45
  |
6 |     let names = vec![String::from("Ada"), String::from("Grace")];
  |         ----- move occurs because `names` has type `Vec<String>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
7 |     let n = total_len(names);
  |                       ----- value moved here
8 |     println!("{n} letters across {} names", names.len());
  |                                             ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
note: consider changing this parameter type in function `total_len` to borrow instead if owning the value isn't necessary
 --> src/main.rs:1:21
  |
1 | fn total_len(names: Vec<String>) -> usize {
  |    ---------        ^^^^^^^^^^^ this parameter takes ownership of the value
  |    |
  |    in this function
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
7 |     let n = total_len(names.clone());
  |                            ++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0382`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. Passing a Vec by value moves it: total_len owns it now, frees it when it returns, and main can't touch it again. Python never has this problem because every variable is a shared reference and a garbage collector cleans up. Rust has no garbage collector. It frees memory at a moment the compiler can see, and ownership is how it sees that moment.

You have three choices whenever a function needs a value:

  • Borrow it (&[Loan], &Loan, &str) when the function only reads. This is the default. Nearly every function you write this week should take its input this way.
  • Borrow it mutably (&mut Vec<Loan>) when the function changes it in place, like sorting.
  • Move it (Vec<Loan>) when the function keeps it or consumes it. Or .clone() it first if you need your own copy, which costs a full copy, every time.

Write &[Loan] rather than &Vec<Loan>. A slice, &[T], is a view of some items in a row, and it accepts a borrowed Vec, an array or part of either. Clippy will tell you this too.

There is one rule for borrows, and the compiler checks it everywhere: a value can have any number of & borrows, or exactly one &mut, but never both at once. Many readers, or one writer. Here a reference is still in use when the code tries to change the list:

fn main() {
    let mut loan_ids = vec![1, 2, 3];
    let first = &loan_ids[0];
    loan_ids.push(4);
    println!("first loan: {first}");
}
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `loan_ids` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
 --> src/main.rs:4:5
  |
3 |     let first = &loan_ids[0];
  |                  -------- immutable borrow occurs here
4 |     loan_ids.push(4);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
5 |     println!("first loan: {first}");
  |                            ----- immutable borrow later used here

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0502`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

The reason is concrete. When a Vec is full, push gets a bigger block of memory, may copy every item across to it, and gives the old block back (under the hood shows this happening). first would still point into the old block, at memory that's no longer the list's. Python can't get into this state, because its garbage collector keeps anything alive while something points at it. C can: the same program compiles and reads whatever is in that memory now. A borrow lasts until the last line that uses it, not to the end of the block, so moving the println! above the push fixes it: first is finished with by then.

Keep some of the rows

To keep the loans that went out before a date, return a Vec of references to the originals instead of copies. The date is fixed, so it lives in a const with a name and a comment, where the next person can find it:

/// Loans that went out before this date count as early.
const CUTOFF: &str = "2026-09-15";

fn out_before_cutoff(loans: &[Loan]) -> Vec<&Loan> {
    loans
        .iter()
        .filter(|loan| loan.status == "out" && loan.loaned_on.as_str() < CUTOFF)
        .collect()
}

Read the return type, Vec<&Loan>, as "some of the same loans you gave me, borrowed, not copied". The compiler knows the references point into loans, because that is the only reference that came in. So the result can't outlive the Vec it borrows from, and the compiler will hold you to that.

loan.loaned_on.as_str() < CUTOFF compares two pieces of text. Leave out the .as_str() and the compiler stops you, with a suggestion:

struct Loan {
    loaned_on: String,
}

/// Loans that went out before this date count as early.
const CUTOFF: &str = "2026-09-15";

fn count_early(loans: &[Loan]) -> usize {
    loans.iter().filter(|loan| loan.loaned_on < CUTOFF).count()
}

fn main() {
    let loans = vec![Loan {
        loaned_on: "2026-08-03".to_string(),
    }];
    println!("{}", count_early(&loans));
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:9:49
  |
9 |     loans.iter().filter(|loan| loan.loaned_on < CUTOFF).count()
  |                                --------------   ^^^^^^- help: try using a conversion method: `.to_string()`
  |                                |                |
  |                                |                expected `String`, found `&str`
  |                                expected because this is `String`

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

< only works between two types that someone has told Rust how to compare, and a String on the left with a &str on the right isn't one of those pairs. loaned_on is a String and CUTOFF is a &str. The suggested CUTOFF.to_string() compiles, and it makes a fresh copy of the date for every loan it checks, only to compare it and throw it away. (Week zero has more on when the compiler's help is wrong.) The cheap fix is on the other side: .as_str() borrows a &str view of the String, so both sides are &str and nothing is copied.

If you pass the date in as a parameter, the compiler asks for a lifetime

With two references coming in, the compiler can't tell which one the results point into:

struct Loan {
    status: String,
    loaned_on: String,
}

fn out_before(loans: &[Loan], cutoff: &str) -> Vec<&Loan> {
    loans
        .iter()
        .filter(|loan| loan.status == "out" && loan.loaned_on.as_str() < cutoff)
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let loans = vec![Loan {
        status: "out".into(),
        loaned_on: "2026-08-11".into(),
    }];
    println!("{}", out_before(&loans, "2026-09-01").len());
}
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> src/main.rs:6:52
  |
6 | fn out_before(loans: &[Loan], cutoff: &str) -> Vec<&Loan> {
  |                      -------          ----         ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `loans` or `cutoff`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
6 | fn out_before<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], cutoff: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a Loan> {
  |              ++++         ++                  ++              ++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0106`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

It needs to know what the returned references borrow from, so it knows how long they stay valid. 'a is a lifetime, a name for "as long as this borrow lasts". The suggested fix compiles, but it's stricter than it needs to be: it ties the result to cutoff as well. The results only point into loans, so only loans needs the label:

fn out_before<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], cutoff: &str) -> Vec<&'a Loan> {
    loans
        .iter()
        .filter(|loan| loan.status == "out" && loan.loaned_on.as_str() < cutoff)
        .collect()
}

Read it as: the &Loans that come out live as long as the loans that went in. Ticket 3 is where lifetimes get properly explained. For now, when the compiler asks, tie the output to the input it really comes from.

Sort

let mut words = vec!["pear", "fig", "kiwi", "apple"];

words.sort_by_key(|w| w.len());
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort_by_key(|w| (w.len(), *w));
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort();
println!("{words:?}");

words.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));
println!("{words:?}");
["fig", "pear", "kiwi", "apple"]
["fig", "kiwi", "pear", "apple"]
["apple", "fig", "kiwi", "pear"]
["pear", "kiwi", "fig", "apple"]
  • sort_by_key sorts by whatever the closure returns. Sorting changes the Vec, so the variable must be declared let mut. Rust variables can't be changed unless they say so, which is why the error in set up happened.
  • The sort is stable: items with equal keys stay in their old order. After the first sort, "pear" still comes before "kiwi" because it did before.
  • A tuple key, (w.len(), *w), sorts by the first part, then breaks ties with the second. Python's key=lambda w: (len(w), w) is the same idea.
  • sort_by takes two items and returns how they compare. b.cmp(a) instead of a.cmp(b) sorts backwards.

Using the pieces together:

println!("out right now: {}", count_out(&loans));

let mut early = out_before_cutoff(&loans);
early.sort_by_key(|loan| (loan.member.as_str(), loan.loan_id));
for loan in &early {
    println!("{} {} {}", loan.member, loan.loan_id, loan.loaned_on);
}
out right now: 3
Alan 3 2026-09-01
Grace 2 2026-08-11

Write a file

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};

fn write_report(path: &str, loans: &[&Loan]) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let file = File::create(path)?;
    let mut out = BufWriter::new(file);
    writeln!(out, "loan_id,member,loaned_on")?;
    for loan in loans {
        writeln!(out, "{},{},{}", loan.loan_id, loan.member, loan.loaned_on)?;
    }
    out.flush()?;
    Ok(())
}

Called with the sorted loans from the example above:

let mut early = out_before_cutoff(&loans);
early.sort_by_key(|loan| (loan.member.as_str(), loan.loan_id));
std::fs::create_dir_all("out")?; // File::create makes files, not folders
write_report("out/early_loans.csv", &early)?;
print!("{}", std::fs::read_to_string("out/early_loans.csv")?);
loan_id,member,loaned_on
3,Alan,2026-09-01
2,Grace,2026-08-11
  • File::create makes or empties the file. BufWriter collects your small writes in memory and hands them to the operating system in big chunks. Without it, every writeln! is a separate request to the OS, which is much slower.
  • writeln! works like println!, but into anything you can write to. Writing can fail (disk full, no permission), so it returns a Result and needs a ?.
  • flush pushes out whatever is still buffered. A BufWriter also flushes when it's dropped, but it has to ignore errors when it does that. Flushing yourself means an error reaches you.
  • std::io::Result<()> is the I/O module's own Result, a type alias like rusqlite's, with its error type filled in.
  • use std::io::Write is there because writeln! into a file and flush come from Write, a trait: a named set of methods that many types share (ticket 3 explains traits). A trait's methods only work where the trait is imported. Forget the line and the error says "items from traits can only be used if the trait is in scope", and its help gives you the use line to add.

File::create makes a file, not the folders it goes in. Point it at a folder that doesn't exist and it fails, with an error that doesn't name the path:

let result = write_report("reports/early_loans.csv", &early);
println!("{result:?}");
Err(Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" })

Through main's ? that prints as Error: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, ... }. That's why the call above runs std::fs::create_dir_all("out")? first: it makes the folder, and does nothing if it's already there. Set up made an out folder in kettle_creek, but a fresh clone of your repository won't have one, because .gitignore leaves it out, so let your program make it too.

Writing CSV by hand works because nothing in this ticket's columns contains a comma. That's a fragile assumption, and ticket 2 replaces it.

Warm-up drills

From here on, the drills and the ticket go in your work project. Wiki examples, in this ticket and later ones, still go in snippets.

cd ~/projects/kettle_creek

Keep drills out of your real program by giving them a program of their own. Cargo treats every file in src/bin/ as a separate program, so put them in src/bin/drills.rs and run cargo run --bin drills from the project folder. With two programs in the project, a bare cargo run no longer knows which one you mean. Tell it, by adding default-run = "kettle_creek" under [package] in Cargo.toml.

Give each drill its own function, such as fn drill_1(db: &Connection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>, and have main open the database and call them in turn. Drills then don't share variables, and you can comment out the call to a drill you've finished. A compile error anywhere still stops the whole file from building, so undo each break-it mistake once you've read the error.

Drill 1. Load suppliers into a Vec of a struct with supplier_id, name, payment_terms_days and active. Print how many there are and how many are active. (rusqlite turns an integer 0 or 1 into a bool for you if the field is a bool.)

24 suppliers, 21 active

Drill 2. Print the five suppliers with the longest payment terms, longest first, breaking ties alphabetically by name. You need sort_by with two comparisons: look up Ordering::then in the docs (hover over cmp in your editor, then follow the return type to its page).

 60 days  Orlin Prairie Motors (9)
 60 days  Sandovar Castings (17)
 45 days  Norrowfield Conveyor Parts (22)
 45 days  Ostrand Hydraulics (3)
 45 days  Pellish Valve Works (11)

Drill 3: break it. Add a state field to your struct and your SELECT, right after name. Now swap name and state in the SELECT, but leave the row.get numbers alone, load the suppliers again (not drill 2's sorted Vec) and print the first one. Then put name first in the SELECT, at index 0, where supplier_id was, and let the error reach main through ?. One mistake compiles and runs, and one fails, but only when it runs:

supplier 1: name = "MO", state = "Quarrow Bearing Co."
Error: InvalidColumnType(0, "name", Text)

The second line is what Rust prints when main returns an error: Error: and then the error's {:?} form, meant for programmers. The same error printed with {} reads Invalid column type Text at index: 0, name: name.

Write in your journal which mistakes the type system caught and which it couldn't. Both columns are text, so Rust has no way to know they're swapped. Types catch a lot, but not this. That's what tests are for, starting in ticket 4.

The ticket

Your program, in src/main.rs, must do all of this. Tick each one off as you go.

Before you type, answer these in your journal. What struct do you need, and which columns can be NULL? What does "open" mean in this table, exactly? What type does the "pick the stale ones" function return? The cutoff date is a fixed number in this ticket: where should it live so the next person can find it? (Look up const.)

Stuck?

Hint 1: which columns, which types

You only need the columns the ticket uses: po_id, supplier_id, buyer, order_date and status. None of those can be NULL in this table (.schema purchase_orders shows NOT NULL), so no Option yet. received_date is the one that would be.

Hint 2: the shape of main

Six or seven lines: open the connection, call the loader, count, call the picker, sort, write, print. If main has a loop in it, something belongs in a function.

Hint 3: sorting references

Your picker returns Vec<&PurchaseOrder>. You can sort that with sort_by_key exactly like a Vec of values. A key of (po.order_date.as_str(), po.po_id) borrows the date instead of copying it. Try po.order_date.clone() as the key instead and notice it compiles but breaks criterion 5.

Sanity checks

These check that you loaded the data properly, not that your answer is right. The review checks the answer.

  • Your Vec holds 2,017 purchase orders. To check counts like these, print them for a moment, println!("{}", pos.len()) or dbg!(pos.len()), and delete the line once they agree.
  • There are 56 POs with status cancelled. Count those with the same .iter().filter(...).count() shape. If you get 56, your loading and filtering work, and the open count uses the same idea.
  • If your program prints 2,017 open POs, the filter isn't running.
  • The CSV's first line is exactly po_id,supplier_id,buyer,order_date, and its dates go up as you read down.

Under the hood

Where your data lives: the stack and the heap

A running program gets memory in two places. The stack holds each function's local variables. It is fast, because making room is just moving a pointer, and limited: every value on it must have a size known when the program is compiled. The heap is a big pool for anything else. You ask for a block of any size while running, and someone has to give it back.

A Vec is both. A Vec in a local variable is three numbers on the stack: a pointer to a block on the heap, how many items are in it (length), and how many fit before it needs a bigger block (capacity). The items themselves sit side by side in that heap block. A String has the same three numbers, pointing at bytes of text.

You can measure this yourself:

use std::mem::size_of;
println!("i64:            {} bytes", size_of::<i64>());
println!("String:         {} bytes", size_of::<String>());
println!("Option<String>: {} bytes", size_of::<Option<String>>());
println!("Loan:           {} bytes", size_of::<Loan>());
println!("Vec<Loan>:      {} bytes", size_of::<Vec<Loan>>());
i64:            8 bytes
String:         24 bytes
Option<String>: 24 bytes
Loan:           104 bytes
Vec<Loan>:      24 bytes

A String is 24 bytes whether it holds "Ada" or a novel: the text is elsewhere. And Option<String> costs nothing extra. Some bit patterns can never be a valid String (its pointer is never null, for one), so Rust uses one of those patterns to mean None. The spare pattern is called a niche.

When a Vec runs out of room, it asks the allocator for a bigger block, and today's implementation roughly doubles it. The standard library doesn't promise the factor. The allocator may grow the block where it is, or hand back a new one and copy everything across. Pushing 2,017 IDs one at a time:

let mut ids: Vec<i64> = Vec::new();
let mut last_cap = ids.capacity();
println!("len {:>4}  capacity {:>4}", ids.len(), last_cap);
for id in 0..2017 {
    ids.push(id);
    if ids.capacity() != last_cap {
        last_cap = ids.capacity();
        println!("len {:>4}  capacity {:>4}", ids.len(), last_cap);
    }
}
len    0  capacity    0
len    1  capacity    4
len    5  capacity    8
len    9  capacity   16
len   17  capacity   32
len   33  capacity   64
len   65  capacity  128
len  129  capacity  256
len  257  capacity  512
len  513  capacity 1024
len 1025  capacity 2048

Ten trips to the allocator for 2,017 pushes. Growing by a constant factor means the total copying is at most a small multiple of the final size, so a push costs a constant amount on average, even though the occasional push may copy everything. That's called amortized O(1). O(1), said "order one", means the cost doesn't grow as the list grows; ticket 3's under the hood explains the notation properly. It's the same reason Python's list.append is fast. If you know the size up front, Vec::with_capacity(n) skips the copying entirely. Ticket 8 measures whether that matters.

Moves now make sense too. Moving a Vec copies its 24 bytes and leaves the heap block where it is. What must never happen is two owners both freeing the same block, and that is the mistake the move error stopped.

Why the dates sort as text

println!("{}", "2026-08-11" < "2026-09-01");
println!("{}", "2025-12-31" < "2026-01-01");
println!("{}", "8/11/2026" < "9/1/2025");
true
true
true

Text compares character by character, left to right, and the first difference decides. That's lexicographic order, the way a dictionary is ordered. A YYYY-MM-DD date puts the most significant part first and pads every part to a fixed width, so text order and time order agree. 8/11/2026 breaks both rules, and so it sorts before September 2025. This is why ISO 8601 exists, why your logs and filenames should use it, and why ticket 4, where the dates aren't ISO, needs a real date type.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Grouping and totals

Group by, without SQL

In SQL this is a GROUP BY. In pandas it's df.groupby("supplier_id")["amount"].agg(["count", "sum"]). In Rust you do it yourself with a HashMap, and once you've done it you'll recognize it inside every groupby you ever call.

A map from keys to values

HashMap<K, V> is Python's dict, with one key type and one value type. It lives in std::collections, so it needs a use:

use std::collections::HashMap;

let mut shelves: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
shelves.insert("fiction", 412);
shelves.insert("history", 158);
shelves.insert("fiction", 415); // same key: replaces the old value

println!("{} keys", shelves.len());
println!("{:?}", shelves.get("history"));
println!("{:?}", shelves.get("poetry"));
2 keys
Some(158)
None

get doesn't return the value. It returns an Option: Some(value) if the key is there, None if it isn't. Python's d[key] raises KeyError at run time. Rust makes "the key might not be there" part of the type, so you decide what happens before the program ever runs. Try to skip that decision and the compiler stops you:

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut members: HashMap<i64, &str> = HashMap::new();
    members.insert(2, "Grace");
    let name: &str = members.get(&2);
    println!("{name}");
}
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:6:22
  |
6 |     let name: &str = members.get(&2);
  |               ----   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `&str`, found `Option<&&str>`
  |               |
  |               expected due to this
  |
  = note: expected reference `&str`
                  found enum `Option<&&str>`
help: consider using `Option::expect` to unwrap the `Option<&&str>` value, panicking if the value is an `Option::None`
  |
6 |     let name: &str = members.get(&2).expect("REASON");
  |                                     +++++++++++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

The suggested .expect("REASON") would compile. It means "crash with this message if the key is missing". That's right when a missing key would be a bug in your program, and wrong when it's something the data can do. Most of the time you want one of these:

match shelves.get("poetry") {
    Some(n) => println!("poetry: {n}"),
    None => println!("no poetry shelf"),
}
if let Some(n) = shelves.get("fiction") {
    println!("fiction: {n}");
}
let poetry = shelves.get("poetry").copied().unwrap_or(0);
println!("poetry, or 0: {poetry}");
no poetry shelf
fiction: 415
poetry, or 0: 0
  • match handles both cases and says what each one does.
  • if let Some(n) = ... is match when you only care about one case.
  • .copied().unwrap_or(0) turns "maybe a reference to a number" into "a number, or 0". copied turns Option<&u32> into Option<u32>. Look up Option in the docs and skim its methods. You'll use a dozen of them by ticket 6.
  • map[&key] also works. It panics if the key is missing, just like Python's d[key]. Use it only where a missing key really is impossible, and you can say why.

Counting and summing: the entry API

The core of every group-by is "find this key's running total, or start one at zero, and add to it". The entry API does that in one lookup:

let words = ["out", "returned", "out", "lost", "out", "returned"];
let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
for w in words {
    *counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1;
}
let mut sorted: Vec<(&str, u32)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
sorted.sort();
println!("{sorted:?}");
[("lost", 1), ("out", 3), ("returned", 2)]

counts.entry(w) finds the slot for w. .or_insert(0) fills it with 0 if it's empty and hands back a mutable reference to the value, and the * in front reaches through that reference so += 1 changes the number in the map. .or_default() does the same with the type's default, which is 0 for numbers. Python's version is counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, or Counter.

A HashMap has no order. To print or write one predictably, collect it into a Vec and sort that. counts.into_iter() walks the map by value: each item is an owned (key, value) pair, and the map is used up, so you can't touch counts afterward. counts.iter() would borrow instead and hand out references, the way for x in &list does. More on why under the hood.

Borrowing a map is what you do when you want to keep it. Each item is then a pair of references, which matters as soon as you compare or add:

let stock: HashMap<&str, (u32, f64)> =
    HashMap::from([("roller chain", (3, 41.5)), ("carriage bolt", (12, 9.0))]);
for (name, (count, value)) in &stock {
    // Borrowing the map hands out references: `count` is a &u32 here.
    if *count > 5 {
        println!("{name}: {count} in stock, worth {value:.2}");
    }
}
let mut pieces = 0;
for &(count, _) in stock.values() {
    // `.values()` borrows just the values. The `&` in the pattern
    // takes the numbers out of the reference.
    pieces += count;
}
println!("{pieces} pieces in all");
carriage bolt: 12 in stock, worth 9.00
15 pieces in all

In the first loop the tuple pattern reaches through the reference, so name, count and value are all references, and comparing needs *count. Printing doesn't care. In the second, &(count, _) matches the reference itself and copies the numbers out, so count is a plain u32. Either works. The three ways to walk any collection, a Vec or a HashMap:

WriteEach item isAfterward
for x in &v, or v.iter()a reference, &T. From a map, a pair of references, (&K, &V)v is unchanged and still yours
for x in &mut v, or v.iter_mut()a mutable reference, &mut T, so *x += 1 changes the item. From a map, (&K, &mut V): values can change, keys never can, so write for (k, v) in &mut map and *v += 1v is still yours, with changed items
for x in v, or v.into_iter()the item itself, T. From a map, the pair (K, V)v is used up

Owned text and borrowed text

Look at the key type: &str, not String. That choice matters more than it looks.

  • String owns its text on the heap. You can keep it as long as you like, change it, and hand it to someone else.
  • &str is a borrowed view of text that somebody else owns: a pointer and a length. It costs nothing to make, but it's only valid while the owner is alive and unchanged.

When your rows are already loaded into a Vec, a map keyed by &str borrows names straight out of those rows, and nothing is copied. A map keyed by String needs its own copy of every key, made with .clone() or .to_string(). For a map that's built, used and thrown away in one function, borrow. For a map that has to outlive the rows it came from, own. The compiler holds you to it:

use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Book {
    title: String,
    shelf: String,
}

fn main() {
    let books = vec![
        Book {
            title: "SICP".into(),
            shelf: "cs".into(),
        },
        Book {
            title: "TAOCP".into(),
            shelf: "cs".into(),
        },
    ];
    let mut per_shelf: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
    for b in &books {
        *per_shelf.entry(b.shelf.as_str()).or_default() += 1;
    }
    drop(books);
    println!("{per_shelf:?}");
}
error[E0505]: cannot move out of `books` because it is borrowed
  --> src/main.rs:23:10
   |
9  |     let books = vec![
   |         ----- binding `books` declared here
...
20 |     for b in &books {
   |              ------ borrow of `books` occurs here
...
23 |     drop(books);
   |          ^^^^^ move out of `books` occurs here
24 |     println!("{per_shelf:?}");
   |                --------- borrow later used here

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0505`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

per_shelf holds views into books, so books can't be thrown away while per_shelf is still in use. The same program in C would compile, then read freed memory and maybe print garbage. Python never has the problem, because its garbage collector keeps the strings alive as long as anything points at them. Rust rejects it before it runs. Ticket 3 gives this rule its proper name.

Switch a map to String keys and the first try usually looks like this:

use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Product {
    category: String,
}

fn per_category(products: &[Product]) -> HashMap<String, usize> {
    let mut counts: HashMap<String, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for p in products {
        *counts.entry(p.category).or_default() += 1;
    }
    counts
}

fn main() {
    let products = vec![Product {
        category: "chain".to_string(),
    }];
    println!("{:?}", per_category(&products));
}
error[E0507]: cannot move out of `p.category` which is behind a shared reference
  --> src/main.rs:10:23
   |
10 |         *counts.entry(p.category).or_default() += 1;
   |                       ^^^^^^^^^^ move occurs because `p.category` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
   |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
   |
10 |         *counts.entry(p.category.clone()).or_default() += 1;
   |                                 ++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0507`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

p is a &Product, a borrow. Handing p.category to entry would move the String out of a product you only borrowed and leave it with a hole where its category was. You can't give away what you borrowed. Here the help is right: .clone() makes the map its own copy of the text. That copy, made once per product, is the cost of an owned key. If the map doesn't need to outlive the rows, keep &str keys and copy nothing.

The same thinking applies to function parameters. Take &str when you only read text, because a string literal already is one and a &String turns into a &str automatically. That conversion is called deref coercion: where the code expects a &str and gets a &String, the compiler lends out the text inside. It's why entry(&p.category) works on a map with &str keys. It only goes that way. A &str never becomes a String without a .to_string().

Putting it together

Total fines per library member. Fines belong to loans, and loans belong to members, so it takes two maps: one to look up a loan's member, and one for the running totals.

use rusqlite::Connection;
use snippets::library;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::error::Error;

struct Loan {
    loan_id: i64,
    member: String,
}

struct Fine {
    loan_id: i64,
    amount: f64,
}

fn load_loans(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Loan>> {
    let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, member FROM loans")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |r| {
        Ok(Loan {
            loan_id: r.get(0)?,
            member: r.get(1)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

fn load_fines(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Fine>> {
    let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, amount FROM fines")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |r| {
        Ok(Fine {
            loan_id: r.get(0)?,
            amount: r.get(1)?,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

/// Total fines per member, with how many fines each.
fn fines_by_member<'a>(loans: &'a [Loan], fines: &[Fine]) -> HashMap<&'a str, (u32, f64)> {
    let member_of: HashMap<i64, &str> = loans
        .iter()
        .map(|l| (l.loan_id, l.member.as_str()))
        .collect();

    let mut totals: HashMap<&str, (u32, f64)> = HashMap::new();
    for fine in fines {
        let member = member_of[&fine.loan_id];
        let entry = totals.entry(member).or_insert((0, 0.0));
        entry.0 += 1;
        entry.1 += fine.amount;
    }
    totals
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let db = library()?;
    let loans = load_loans(&db)?;
    let fines = load_fines(&db)?;
    let totals = fines_by_member(&loans, &fines);

    let mut rows: Vec<(&str, u32, f64)> = totals
        .into_iter()
        .map(|(m, (n, total))| (m, n, total))
        .collect();
    rows.sort_by(|a, b| b.2.total_cmp(&a.2).then_with(|| a.0.cmp(b.0)));

    for (member, n, total) in &rows {
        println!("{member:<7} {n} fines  {total:>6.2}   (unformatted: {total})");
    }
    Ok(())
}
Ada     3 fines   25.25   (unformatted: 25.25)
Grace   3 fines    1.10   (unformatted: 1.1)
  • member_of is built with .map(...).collect(). Iterators of pairs collect straight into a HashMap.
  • member_of[&fine.loan_id] panics on a missing key. Here every fine was made from a loan, so a missing one would be a bug. In your ticket, think about whether an invoice can name a supplier that isn't in suppliers, and what the report should do if it does.
  • The value is a tuple, (u32, f64): a count and a total, updated through entry.0 and entry.1. A small struct with named fields reads better once there are three or more.
  • fines_by_member has a lifetime 'a on loans and on the output, for the reason you met in ticket 1: the keys of the result are borrowed from loans.

Sorting by a float

The sort line uses total_cmp, not sort_by_key. Here's why:

fn main() {
    let mut totals = vec![("Ada", 25.25), ("Grace", 1.1), ("Alan", 0.0)];
    totals.sort_by_key(|t| t.1);
    println!("{totals:?}");
}

3   |     totals.sort_by_key(|t| t.1);
    |            ^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `Ord` is not implemented for `{float}`
    |
    = help: the following other types implement trait `Ord`:
              i128
              i16
              i32
              i64
              i8
              isize
              u128
              u16
            and 4 others
note: required by a bound in `slice::<impl [T]>::sort_by_key`
   --> ~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/src/rust/library/alloc/src/slice.rs:252:12
    |
249 |     pub fn sort_by_key<K, F>(&mut self, mut f: F)
    |            ----------- required by a bound in this associated function
...
252 |         K: Ord,
    |            ^^^ required by this bound in `slice::<impl [T]>::sort_by_key`

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

sort_by_key needs a key that implements Ord, a total order, where any two values compare as less, equal or greater. Floats don't have one, because of NaN ("not a number", what 0.0 / 0.0 gives you). NaN is not less than, equal to or greater than anything, itself included. Python sorts floats anyway and gives you a wrong order, without a word, if a NaN sneaks in. Rust makes you choose. a.total_cmp(&b) is a total order on floats that puts NaN at the ends, which is what you want for sorting. .then_with(|| ...) breaks ties with a second comparison, just like the tuple keys in ticket 1.

Formatting money

The output above prints each total twice: {total:>6.2} right-aligns it in six characters with two decimals, and plain {total} prints the shortest decimal that reads back as exactly the same float. On this tiny library they agree. On a quarter's invoices they won't, and you'll see digits like ...55000000002. That's not a bug in your code: it's what floating point does. For this report, format with two decimals and move on. Ticket 3 is where it stops being cosmetic.

Writing real CSV

To try this in your snippets project, run cargo add csv there first. Every line ends in ?, so it goes in a main that returns Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>, as in ticket 1. The crate handles quoting for you. Any field with a comma, a quote or a line break gets wrapped in quotes, and quotes inside get doubled, which is the rule every spreadsheet program expects:

let path = "books.csv";
let mut w = csv::Writer::from_path(path)?;
w.write_record(["book_id", "title", "fines"])?;
w.write_record(["101", "The Mythical Man-Month", "0.30"])?;
w.write_record(["106", "Programming Pearls, 2nd ed.", "1.10"])?;
w.write_record(["107", "The \"Dragon Book\"", "0.00"])?;
let total = 1.1_f64;
w.write_record(["108".to_string(), "Code".to_string(), format!("{total:.2}")])?;
w.flush()?;
book_id,title,fines
101,The Mythical Man-Month,0.30
106,"Programming Pearls, 2nd ed.",1.10
107,"The ""Dragon Book""",0.00
108,Code,1.10

write_record takes any list of things that look like text, such as string literals or Strings, as long as every field in one record has the same type. That's why the last record turns everything into a String. format! is println! that gives you the String instead of printing it. The csv crate can also write structs directly through serde, but that's more machinery than this ticket needs.

One function per report

When you move ticket 1 out of main, its function opens a file and reads the database, so it can fail in two ways: an I/O error or a rusqlite error. A function can only name one error type, and ? refuses to pass along an error that doesn't fit it. The same thing on a smaller scale, a function that parses a number and writes a file:

use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;

// Reads a count typed on a slip and writes it to a report.
fn count_report(path: &str, typed: &str) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let count: u32 = typed.trim().parse()?;
    let mut file = File::create(path)?;
    writeln!(file, "count,{count}")?;
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    println!("{:?}", count_report("count.csv", " 12 "));
}

  |                                   this can't be annotated with `?` because it has type `Result<_, ParseIntError>`

The function promised std::io::Result, which can only carry an I/O error, and parse fails with a ParseIntError. The fix you already know from main: return Box<dyn Error>, "any kind of error", and ? will box whichever error turns up.

use std::error::Error;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;

// Reads a count typed on a slip and writes it to a report.
fn count_report(path: &str, typed: &str) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let count: u32 = typed.trim().parse()?;
    let mut file = File::create(path)?;
    writeln!(file, "count,{count}")?;
    Ok(())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    count_report("count.csv", " 12 ")?;
    println!("{:?}", count_report("count.csv", "twelve"));
    Ok(())
}
Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })

Use it for every report function this week. Ticket 5 replaces it with an error type of your own, which can say which kind of error happened.

Drill 1. Count products per category with a HashMap<&str, usize> whose keys borrow from your loaded rows. Print alphabetically.

Drill 2. The three suppliers with the highest average list price across their products, with how many products each. You need a count and a sum per supplier, then a division, then a float sort. Look up supplier names with a second map. The division is an f64 sum over a whole-number count, so one side needs as f64 (from week zero).

Saltreu Pneumatics           9 products, average list price 210.18
Pellish Valve Works          8 products, average list price 199.86
Kestrin Filtration           6 products, average list price 110.61

Drill 3: break it. In drill 1's function, add drop(products); (or whatever you called the Vec) between building the map and printing it. drop frees a value right away instead of at the end of its block. Read the error, then change the map to HashMap<String, usize> so it owns its keys. What did you have to add inside the loop, and what does that cost for 176 products? For a million?

The ticket

Before you type, answer these in your journal. What is the key of your grouping map, and what is the value? Should the key be the supplier's ID or its name, and what goes wrong with names? Do you need the supplier name during grouping, or only when writing? How will you test "July 1 through September 30" at the edges, and is <= "2026-09-30" right for a date written as text? (If you write the test as two comparisons joined by &&, clippy will suggest a range with contains instead. Week zero shows both.)

Stuck?

Hint 1: two maps

One map from supplier ID to name, built from the suppliers. One map from supplier ID to a running count and total, built from the invoices. Group by the ID, which is unique and never misspelled, and look up the name only when you write each row.

Hint 2: from map to sorted rows

Turn the totals map into a Vec with into_iter().collect(), then sort it with sort_by: compare totals with total_cmp (which way round puts the biggest first?), then then_with on the names.

Hint 3: the missing supplier

The choices are: skip the invoice (and the total no longer ties to the ledger), keep it under a placeholder name like "(unknown supplier 99)", or stop the program with an error. Which one would Priya want? names.get(&id) gives you an Option to make that choice with.

If you choose the placeholder and write names.get(&id).copied().unwrap_or(&format!(...)), the compiler refuses. Which message you get depends on where the name goes. Used later in the same function, it's "temporary value dropped while borrowed" (E0716). Returned from a function, it's "cannot return value referencing temporary value" (E0515). The cause is the same: format! makes a new String that nothing keeps, so it's freed at the end of the statement, and the &str you borrowed from it can't outlive it. One way out is to make the name owned at the point where you write each output row: one String per supplier row is a couple of dozen small copies at most, which is nothing. Criterion 6 is about the loop over invoices, which runs once per invoice, not about the few rows you write.

Sanity checks

  • You load 1,745 invoices and 24 suppliers.
  • One row to check your arithmetic and your date filter against: Quarrow Bearing Co., supplier 1, has 25 invoices totaling 85542.55 in Q3. Printed with a plain {}, that total comes out as 85542.55000000002.
  • Not every supplier billed us in Q3, so your CSV has fewer than 24 rows.
  • Run it twice and compare the files with diff. If they differ, something depends on HashMap order.

Hand it in

Under the hood

How a hash table finds things

A HashMap is an array of slots called buckets. To store a key, it runs the key through a hash function, which turns any value into a big number that looks random but is always the same for the same key. Then it uses part of that number to pick a bucket. To find the key again, it hashes it again and looks in the same place. No searching, so lookups take about the same time with ten keys or ten million: O(1) on average.

use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;
use std::hash::{Hash, Hasher};

let buckets = 8;
for member in ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan", "Edsger"] {
    let mut h = DefaultHasher::new();
    member.hash(&mut h);
    let hash = h.finish();
    println!("{member:<7} hash {hash:>20}  bucket {}", hash % buckets);
}
Ada     hash 17390174587215729682  bucket 2
Grace   hash  4016552697901753768  bucket 0
Alan    hash 10154332038248538411  bucket 3
Edsger  hash  6817028703008280599  bucket 7

Two keys can land in the same bucket. That's a collision, and every hash table has a plan for it: look in the next free slot, or keep a little list per bucket. Collisions are why the table keeps spare room. When it gets too full (Rust's table grows when it's seven-eighths full), it allocates a bigger array and moves every key, the same doubling trick as Vec. Rust's HashMap is a port of Google's SwissTable design, which checks sixteen slots at a time with single CPU instructions.

Why the order changes every run

The example above used DefaultHasher::new(), which always hashes the same way, so its output is the same every time. A real HashMap doesn't. Each one gets a hasher with secret random keys, seeded from the operating system. So the same names land in different buckets on different runs, and iterating the map gives a different order.

This is deliberate. If a web server's hash function is fixed and public, an attacker can send thousands of keys built to land in one bucket, and every lookup becomes a slow search through all of them. That's called hash flooding, or HashDoS. In 2011 researchers showed it working against most of the popular web platforms of the day. A secret random key per map stops it, and the hash Rust uses, SipHash, was designed so the keys can't be worked out from outside.

The lesson for your reports: never let output order depend on a HashMap. Sort first. Python's dict keeps insertion order, which hides this habit until you work in a language that doesn't.

Sorting, and what stable means

Comparison sorts, the kind that work by asking "is a before b?", need about n log n comparisons for n items, and it's been proved that none can do better in general. For a report of a couple of dozen rows that's nothing. For ten million rows it's the difference between seconds and hours, compared with a naive sort that needs n².

sort, sort_by and sort_by_key are stable: equal items keep their original order. Since Rust 1.81 they use a merge sort variant called driftsort. sort_unstable and friends can reorder equal items, use no extra memory, and are often faster. Stability matters when you sort twice: sort by name, then stable-sort by total, and suppliers with equal totals stay alphabetical. Your tie-break with then_with gets the same result in one sort, and it says so in the code.

Go deeper

  • The Rust Book, chapter 8.2: Strings and 8.3: Hash Maps.
  • The std::collections docs, especially "When Should You Use Which Collection?" and the table of operation costs.
  • The Option docs. Read the method list once; you'll come back to it.
  • The csv crate's tutorial, by its author, Andrew Gallant. It's a model of how to document a library.
  • Matt Kulukundis, "Designing a Fast, Efficient, Cache-friendly Hash Table, Step by Step", CppCon 2017. The talk that introduced SwissTable. It's about C++, but the ideas are the ones inside Rust's HashMap.
  • Introduction to Algorithms (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein), chapter 11 on hash tables and chapter 8 on the n log n lower bound for sorting. The standard reference: dense, and worth it in small doses.

Ticket 3: invoices that don't match

From
Dana Whitlock, Operations Manager
To
You
Cc
Priya Raman, Accounts Payable
Date
Monday, October 12, 2026, 7:58 AM
Subject
Invoices that don't match their POs

Thanks for the spend report. Priya used it on Thursday's supplier call.

Now the one that matters. Every month we pay a few invoices we shouldn't. Priya's team checks a sample by hand. I want every PO checked against every invoice. Main branch only for now (branch is MAIN): Millbrook's invoices are still in their old system.

What a PO should cost: add up its lines, quantity times unit price.

What we were billed: add up the PO's invoices. One catch. Suppliers sometimes send the same invoice twice and we key in both. If a PO has two invoices with the same invoice number, the one entered later (the higher invoice_id) is a duplicate: don't count it, report it. Two different invoice numbers that add up to the PO's total are fine; some suppliers bill in parts.

Report these, in this order:

  1. ORPHAN_INVOICE: an invoice whose PO number doesn't exist at all. Usually a typo when it was keyed in.
  2. DUPLICATE_INVOICE: the extra copies described above, one row per extra copy.
  3. BILLED_CANCELLED: a canceled PO with any invoices. We owe nothing on those.
  4. BILLED_OPEN: an open PO that's been invoiced. Shouldn't happen. I want to know if it does.
  5. OVERBILLED: a received PO billed more than it should cost.
  6. UNDERBILLED: a received PO billed less. Often a short shipment, but I still want to see it.
  7. NOT_INVOICED: a received PO with no invoice at all. Suppliers get 30 days, so only POs received on or before September 4.

A received PO billed exactly right isn't on the report.

Send it as discrepancies.csv with columns kind, po_id, invoice_number, supplier, expected, billed, difference:

  • supplier is the name. invoice_number is only filled in on orphan and duplicate rows.
  • expected is what the PO should cost. Put 0.00 for a canceled PO, and leave it blank on orphan and duplicate rows, where there's nothing to compare.
  • billed is what we were billed for the PO. On an orphan or duplicate row, it's that one invoice's amount.
  • difference is billed minus expected, blank when expected is blank.
  • Money with two decimals, no dollar sign. Sort by kind in the order above, then po_id, then invoice_number.

When it runs, print how many of each kind it found and the total overbilled (the sum of the differences on OVERBILLED rows).

Priya will check your numbers against her sample, to the cent. So to the cent it has to be. The wiki page is here.

Dana

This ticket teaches enums that carry data, exhaustive match (on two values at once, too), fold, derives, a money type of your own with operator traits, HashSet, Option combinators, let-else and lifetimes properly. Under the hood: how a float stores 0.1, big-O and the hash join, and what a database index is. Crates allowed: rusqlite, csv.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Types that model the business

Make wrong answers hard to write

Ticket 2 was arithmetic. This one is judgment: every PO lands in exactly one of several outcomes, money has to be exact, and three tables have to be lined up against each other. Rust's answer to all three is the same idea: put the rules into types, so the compiler checks them every time you build. The library examples below have the same shapes as the ticket, on different data.

An enum for "exactly one of these"

An enum lists every possible form a value can take. Unlike a Python Enum, each variant can carry its own data:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
enum Standing {
    Lost,
    Overdue { days: i64 },
    Out,
    Returned,
}

A Standing is Lost, or Overdue with a number of days attached, or Out, or Returned. Never two at once, and never a value that isn't on the list. A string like "overdue" can be misspelled, and the misspelling compiles; Standing::Overdu does not.

You take an enum apart with match:

fn action(standing: Standing) -> String {
    match standing {
        Standing::Lost => "bill the replacement".to_string(),
        Standing::Overdue { days } if days > 30 => format!("{days} days late: send a letter"),
        Standing::Overdue { days } => format!("{days} days late: send a reminder"),
        Standing::Out => "nothing yet".to_string(),
        Standing::Returned => "nothing".to_string(),
    }
}
  • Standing::Overdue { days } matches the variant and pulls its days out into a variable, in one step.
  • if days > 30 after a pattern is a guard: the arm only matches when the condition holds too. Arms are tried top to bottom, so the 40-day loan takes the first Overdue arm and the 3-day loan falls through to the second.
  • A match is an expression. Each arm produces a value, and the whole match is the function's return value.
let mut all = vec![
    Standing::Returned,
    Standing::Overdue { days: 3 },
    Standing::Lost,
    Standing::Out,
    Standing::Overdue { days: 40 },
];
all.sort();
for s in &all {
    println!("{:<26} {}", format!("{s:?}"), action(*s));
}
let late = all
    .iter()
    .filter(|s| matches!(s, Standing::Overdue { .. }))
    .count();
println!("{late} overdue");
Lost                       bill the replacement
Overdue { days: 3 }        3 days late: send a reminder
Overdue { days: 40 }       40 days late: send a letter
Out                        nothing yet
Returned                   nothing
2 overdue

Why format!("{s:?}") inside the println!? A derived Debug doesn't pad the value as a whole: {:<26?} leaves Lost unpadded and pads the 3 inside Overdue { days: 3 }. So the line turns the value into a String first, and a String pads properly. matches!(value, pattern) is a one-line match that answers yes or no. Overdue { .. } means "the Overdue variant, whatever its fields are".

The rule that makes enums worth it: a match must cover every variant. Leave one out and the program doesn't build:

enum Standing {
    Lost,
    Overdue { days: i64 },
    Out,
    Returned,
}

fn action(standing: Standing) -> String {
    match standing {
        Standing::Lost => "bill the replacement".to_string(),
        Standing::Overdue { days } => format!("{days} days late"),
        Standing::Returned => "nothing".to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", action(Standing::Out));
}
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `Standing::Out` not covered
 --> src/main.rs:9:11
  |
9 |     match standing {
  |           ^^^^^^^^ pattern `Standing::Out` not covered
  |
note: `Standing` defined here
 --> src/main.rs:1:6
  |
1 | enum Standing {
  |      ^^^^^^^^
...
4 |     Out,
  |     --- not covered
  = note: the matched value is of type `Standing`
help: ensure that all possible cases are being handled by adding a match arm with a wildcard pattern or an explicit pattern as shown
  |
12~         Standing::Returned => "nothing".to_string(),
13~         Standing::Out => todo!(),
  |

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0004`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

This is the compiler keeping a list for you. Add a variant next month and every match that forgot about it becomes an error you have to fix before anything runs. Python's match statement doesn't check this when it runs (a type checker can, if you set it up), and an if/elif chain simply falls off the end. A catch-all arm, _ => ..., turns the check off for that match. Sometimes that's right. In code that decides what to report, it means a new case gets silently reported as nothing.

From text to an enum

The database stores a status as text, and your code wants an enum. The conversion is a match on the text:

use std::error::Error;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum LoanStatus {
    Out,
    Returned,
    Lost,
}

fn loan_status(text: &str) -> Option<LoanStatus> {
    match text {
        "out" => Some(LoanStatus::Out),
        "returned" => Some(LoanStatus::Returned),
        "lost" => Some(LoanStatus::Lost),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn require_status(text: &str) -> Result<LoanStatus, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let status = loan_status(text).ok_or_else(|| format!("unknown loan status {text:?}"))?;
    Ok(status)
}
println!("{:?}", loan_status("out"));
println!("{:?}", loan_status("Lost"));
match require_status("Lost") {
    Ok(status) => println!("{status:?}"),
    Err(e) => println!("error: {e}"),
}
Some(Out)
None
error: unknown loan status "Lost"
  • Here the _ arm belongs. Text can be anything, so "anything else" has to be handled, and it becomes None. That's the one place a catch-all is right: where the outside world comes in. Once you have a LoanStatus, every match on it lists the variants by name.
  • The match is case-sensitive. "Lost" isn't "lost". Whether that's right depends on the data, so look at what your column really holds.
  • ok_or_else turns None into an error, built by the closure only when it's needed. A String converts into a Box<dyn Error>, so ? can return it from any function with that return type. Load the status as a String, as in ticket 1, and convert each row in a second step after loading. An unknown status then stops the program with a message that names the value.

Matching on two things at once

Some decisions depend on two values. Put them in a tuple and match on the tuple: each arm is a pattern for both at once. Here a loan's verdict depends on its status and on how its days out compare with the 14-day limit:

use std::cmp::Ordering;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
enum LoanStatus {
    Out,
    Returned,
    Lost,
}

const LOAN_DAYS: i64 = 14;

fn verdict(status: LoanStatus, days_out: i64) -> &'static str {
    match (status, days_out.cmp(&LOAN_DAYS)) {
        (LoanStatus::Lost, _) => "bill the replacement",
        (LoanStatus::Out, Ordering::Greater) => "overdue: send a reminder",
        (LoanStatus::Out, Ordering::Less | Ordering::Equal) => "out, not due yet",
        (LoanStatus::Returned, Ordering::Greater) => "returned late: fine it",
        (LoanStatus::Returned, Ordering::Less | Ordering::Equal) => "returned on time",
    }
}
let loans = [
    (LoanStatus::Out, 3),
    (LoanStatus::Out, 20),
    (LoanStatus::Returned, 14),
    (LoanStatus::Returned, 15),
    (LoanStatus::Lost, 2),
];
for (status, days) in loans {
    println!(
        "{:<9} {days:>2} days: {}",
        format!("{status:?}"),
        verdict(status, days)
    );
}
Out        3 days: out, not due yet
Out       20 days: overdue: send a reminder
Returned  14 days: returned on time
Returned  15 days: returned late: fine it
Lost       2 days: bill the replacement
  • a.cmp(&b) compares two values and returns a std::cmp::Ordering: Less, Equal or Greater. It's an enum like any other, so it can go in a pattern.
  • Ordering::Less | Ordering::Equal is an or-pattern: the arm matches either one.
  • (LoanStatus::Lost, _) means "lost, and any Ordering". A _ inside a tuple only waves through that one position. Every status is still named, so a new LoanStatus variant would still be a compile error here. That's different from a whole-arm _ =>, which waves through everything.
  • -> &'static str returns text written into the program itself, like "bill the replacement". Text like that is never freed, and 'static is the lifetime that says so. It needs no input to borrow from, which is why this function can return a &str without a 'a. Ticket 6 says more.
  • The compiler checks every combination. Delete the Returned, Greater arm and it names the missing pair, with its full path: (LoanStatus::Returned, std::cmp::Ordering::Greater) not covered.

What each derive buys you

The #[derive(...)] line asks the compiler to write standard behavior for your type. Each one is a trait, a named ability, that other code can rely on:

DeriveWhat you getWhy you'd want it here
DebugPrinting with {:?}Seeing what you have while you work
Clone, Copy.clone(); and with Copy, plain assignment copies instead of movingSmall values like a kind or an amount should behave like numbers. Copy is only allowed when every field is Copy, so not for a String
PartialEq, Eq== and !=Comparing kinds and amounts
PartialOrd, Ord<, .cmp(), .sort()For an enum the order is the order you declared the variants in. That's why Lost sorted first above
HashUsable as a HashMap key or in a HashSetCounting per kind
DefaultA zero value, T::default()What entry(...).or_default() starts from

Declaration order as sort order is worth noticing. If your report must list kinds in a set order, declare the enum's variants in that order and derive Ord: then sorting is correct by construction, and nobody has to keep a separate list of strings in step with the enum.

Why PartialEq and Eq are two things: floats. f64 has NaN, which isn't equal even to itself, so f64 can only be PartialEq. And because it isn't Eq or Hash, it can't be a HashMap key:

use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let mut by_price: HashMap<f64, &str> = HashMap::new();
    by_price.insert(0.30, "loan 4");
    println!("{:?}", by_price.get(&0.30));
}

  |
