Under the hood

Information hiding

In 1972 David Parnas published a short paper, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules". He took one small program and split it into modules two ways. The first followed the steps of the program, the way most people would: read the input, process it, write the output. The second gave each module one design decision that was likely to change, and hid that decision behind the module's interface. Then he asked what each version would cost to change. In the first, most changes touched most modules, because every step knew how the data was stored. In the second, most changes stayed inside one module.

That's the test to put to your own layout. Next year Millbrook might send CSV files instead of a table. Priya might want a dispute status on each discrepancy. Money might need a currency. For each change, count the files you would have to open. If db.rs is the only file that knows the data lives in SQLite, a new source of rows changes one file and adds another. If Cents keeps its i64 private, the day it needs a currency field, nobody outside money.rs notices.

John Ousterhout's word for a good module is deep: a small interface with a lot of work behind it. parse_amount(&str) -> Result<Cents, AmountError> is deep. It's one function with one input, hiding signs, commas, parentheses and the cents rule. A module that makes every helper pub is shallow, because its callers have to learn everything it knows.

What cargo actually compiles

The Rust compiler, rustc, works on one crate at a time. A crate is the unit of compilation: rustc starts at lib.rs or main.rs, follows every mod line to the files they name, and compiles the whole tree as one piece. Modules are walls and names inside that piece. Python works differently: it compiles each file separately, when the running program first imports it.

Your package now holds several crates. Cargo compiles the library first. Then it compiles main.rs as a second crate that links to the library, and each file in tests/ as one more crate that does the same. That's why main.rs sees only what's pub: to the compiler it is outside code, exactly like a test. It's also why cargo test printed four sections above. Between builds, rustc keeps notes in target/ about what it already compiled (incremental compilation), so a one-line change doesn't redo everything. Big projects go further and split into many crates in a workspace, so cargo can compile independent crates at the same time and skip the ones that didn't change.

A diff is a test

Your ../out_before folder is what's called a golden file test: save output that's known to be good, and compare every new run against it. Michael Feathers calls tests like this characterization tests, in Working Effectively with Legacy Code. They pin down what code does today, right or wrong, so you can change it safely. They're cheap to write and catch any change at all, which makes them the right tool for a refactor. A bug fix is different: it's supposed to change the output, and the old golden file can't tell a fix from a mistake. There you read the new output, check the change is the one you meant, and save it as the new golden file. They're brittle too, when output contains something that changes every run, like a timestamp. Ticket 6's workbook has one. Unit tests say why each rule exists. A golden file says only that nothing moved, and during a refactor that's the one thing you need to know.

Go deeper

  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 7: Packages, Crates and Modules. Read it after your refactor, when the words will mean something.
  • Chapter 11.3: Test Organization, on unit and integration tests side by side.
  • The Cargo Book: Package Layout, where src/bin, tests, examples and benches go.
  • thiserror and anyhow: what most teams use instead of hand-written error code. thiserror is for libraries, where callers need to match on variants. anyhow is for programs, where errors mostly get reported. Now that you've written the code yourself, read their front pages and see what each one would write for you.
  • The Rust API Guidelines, interoperability, especially "Error types are meaningful and well-behaved".
  • David Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules" (Communications of the ACM, 1972). Six pages, and still the best argument for how to split a program.
  • A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout, chapter 4, "Modules Should Be Deep". The bookshelf has more on it.
  • Refactoring, 2nd edition, by Martin Fowler (2018), chapters 1 and 2, and Working Effectively with Legacy Code by Michael Feathers (2004), for changing code you're afraid of.

This ticket teaches traits, generics with trait bounds, trait objects, a real command-line interface with clap, writing Excel files, and exit codes. Under the hood: how generics and trait objects compile, what an .xlsx file really is, and how processes report failure. Crates allowed: rusqlite, csv, rust_xlsxwriter, clap.

Engineering wiki / Rust / Interfaces, command lines and workbooks

One function for every table

Three of the four sheets are tables: a header row, then one row per item, each item a different type. You could write three nearly identical functions. This page shows how to write one, and how to give the program a command line that refuses bad input. First, the new crates:

cargo add rust_xlsxwriter
cargo add clap --features derive

cargo add changes only the project you run it in. Run both lines in snippets for the examples, and again in kettle_creek for the drills and the ticket.

A trait is a promise

A trait names a set of methods that a type promises to have. You've been using traits since ticket 1: Debug, Display, Ord and Iterator are all traits. Now you write one. Here is a trait for anything that can be one row of a table, on the library toy:

/// Anything that can be shown as one row of a table.
trait TableRow {
    /// Column names. The same for every row of a type, so no `self`.
    fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str];
    /// This row's cells, in header order.
    fn cells(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

headers has no self: it belongs to the type, not to any one row, because every book has the same columns. It's called an associated function, and you call it on the type, as Book::headers(), the same way you've called Bin::new since week zero.

Its return type, &'static [&'static str], reads from the inside out:

  • &str is borrowed text, and &[&str] is a borrowed list of those: a slice, as in week zero.
  • 'static is a lifetime, like ticket 3's 'a, but a fixed one: "good for the whole run of the program". It's the longest there is.
  • String literals such as "title" are &'static str, because they're stored inside the program file itself and never freed. A list written out of literals, &["book_id", "title"], is 'static too.

So headers can hand out its list without anyone owning it, and the caller can keep it as long as it likes. cells takes &self, so it's an ordinary method that reads one row. Implementing the trait is where each type keeps its promise:

impl TableRow for Book {
    fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str] {
        &["book_id", "title", "author"]
    }
    fn cells(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        vec![
            self.book_id.to_string(),
            self.title.clone(),
            self.author.clone(),
        ]
    }
}

impl TableRow for Loan {
    fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str] {
        &["loan_id", "member", "status"]
    }
    fn cells(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        vec![
            self.loan_id.to_string(),
            self.member.clone(),
            self.status.clone(),
        ]
    }
}

Python's nearest relative is a Protocol from typing, or an abstract base class. The difference is that Python checks a protocol only if you run a type checker, and only as a hint. Rust checks every use of the trait, at compile time, every time.

One function, many types

fn print_table<T: TableRow>(rows: &[T]) {
    println!("{}", T::headers().join(" | "));
    for row in rows {
        println!("{}", row.cells().join(" | "));
    }
}

<T: TableRow> says "T can be any type, as long as it implements TableRow". T is a type parameter, and : TableRow is its bound. Inside the function you can use exactly what the bound promises and nothing else: T::headers() and row.cells(). Calling it with two different types:

books and loans below are loaders you could write by now: one SELECT into a Vec, as in ticket 1, with Book holding an author as well this time.

let books = books(&db)?;
let loans = loans(&db)?;
print_table(&books[..2]);
println!();
print_table(&loans[..3]);
book_id | title | author
101 | The Mythical Man-Month | Brooks
102 | Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs | Abelson

loan_id | member | status
1 | Ada | returned
2 | Grace | out
3 | Alan | out

The bound isn't a formality. Hand the function a type that never made the promise, and the compiler says so at the call:

trait TableRow {
    fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str];
    fn cells(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

fn print_table<T: TableRow>(rows: &[T]) {
    println!("{}", T::headers().join(" | "));
    for row in rows {
        println!("{}", row.cells().join(" | "));
    }
}

struct Fine {
    loan_id: i64,
    cents: i64,
}

fn main() {
    let fines = vec![Fine {
        loan_id: 6,
        cents: 2495,
    }];
    print_table(&fines);
}
error[E0277]: the trait bound `Fine: TableRow` is not satisfied
  --> src/main.rs:23:17

23 |     print_table(&fines);
   |     ----------- ^^^^^^ the trait `TableRow` is not implemented for `Fine`
   |     |
   |     required by a bound introduced by this call
   |

  --> src/main.rs:1:1

1  | trait TableRow {
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
note: required by a bound in `print_table`
  --> src/main.rs:6:19

6  | fn print_table<T: TableRow>(rows: &[T]) {

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

Read the last note: the error points at the call and at the bound that requires it. That pairing is how you find out what a library function wants from your types.

A word on .clone() in cells. Each cell becomes a new String because the trait says Vec<String>. That's a copy of every piece of text per row, which is fine for a few thousand rows in a report. A trait that hands a writer each cell directly, the way the ticket's sheets will need to anyway, avoids the copies. Notice that the trait's signature decides the cost for every type that implements it. Designing a trait means choosing that cost.

When the type isn't known until the program runs

A generic function needs one type per call: a &[Book] or a &[Loan], never a mix. Sometimes you need a list of different types side by side. That's a trait object, written dyn Trait:

trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}

struct Book {
    title: String,
}

struct Fine {
    cents: i64,
}

impl Describe for Book {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("book: {}", self.title)
    }
}

impl Describe for Fine {
    fn describe(&self) -> String {
        format!("fine: {}.{:02}", self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100)
    }
}

fn describe_all(items: &[Box<dyn Describe>]) {
    for item in items {
        println!("{}", item.describe());
    }
}
let items: Vec<Box<dyn Describe>> = vec![
    Box::new(Book {
        title: "The Mythical Man-Month".to_string(),
    }),
    Box::new(Fine { cents: 2495 }),
    Box::new(Book {
        title: "A Discipline of Programming".to_string(),
    }),
];
describe_all(&items);
book: The Mythical Man-Month
fine: 24.95
book: A Discipline of Programming

Box<dyn Describe> means "a value on the heap, of some type that implements Describe, and we've forgotten which". The values have different sizes, so they can't sit side by side in a Vec directly. Each goes in its own Box on the heap, and the Vec holds the pointers. The cost is a heap allocation per item and an indirect call per method call. Under the hood shows what that call looks like.

Not every trait can be used this way. Try it with TableRow:

trait TableRow {
    fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str];
    fn cells(&self) -> Vec<String>;
}

fn print_rows(_rows: &[Box<dyn TableRow>]) {}

fn main() {}
error[E0038]: the trait `TableRow` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:6:28
  |
6 | fn print_rows(_rows: &[Box<dyn TableRow>]) {}
  |                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^ `TableRow` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:8
  |
1 | trait TableRow {
  |       -------- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str];
  |        ^^^^^^^ ...because associated function `headers` has no `self` parameter
help: consider turning `headers` into a method by giving it a `&self` argument
  |
2 |     fn headers(&self) -> &'static [&'static str];
  |                +++++
help: alternatively, consider constraining `headers` so it does not apply to trait objects
  |
2 |     fn headers() -> &'static [&'static str] where Self: Sized;
  |                                             +++++++++++++++++

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0038`.
error: could not compile `snippets` (bin "snippets") due to 1 previous error

A trait object only knows a value, not its type. headers() has no value to ask, so there would be nothing to call it on. That's what "dyn compatible" means: every method has to be callable through a value, unless it opts out of trait objects with where Self: Sized, which is what the compiler's help above suggests. Sized means "a type whose size is known when the program is compiled", which every ordinary type is and a dyn value isn't. So a method with that bound exists on Book and Loan, and simply isn't offered on a dyn TableRow.

For the pack, generics are the right fit. Each sheet holds one type of row, known when you write the code, and headers naturally belongs to the type. Reach for dyn when the set of types really is open or mixed at run time: plugins, a list of different shapes, error types from several libraries (that's what Box<dyn Error> in main has been doing since ticket 1).

A real command line

clap's derive style turns a struct into an argument parser. The field types say what each argument is, and the doc comments become the help text:

use clap::Parser;

/// Fines report for the lending library.
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(name = "fines")]
struct Cli {
    /// Shelf to report on: one capital letter and one or two digits, like B12.
    #[arg(long, value_parser = parse_shelf)]
    shelf: String,

    /// Only this member's fines.
    #[arg(long)]
    member: Option<String>,

    /// Where to write the workbook.
    #[arg(long, default_value = "out/fines.xlsx")]
    out: String,
}

/// Accept `B12` or `C7`; refuse anything else, saying why.
fn parse_shelf(s: &str) -> Result<String, String> {
    let mut chars = s.chars();
    let Some(letter) = chars.next() else {
        return Err("a shelf code can't be empty".to_string());
    };
    if !letter.is_ascii_uppercase() {
        return Err(format!("{s:?} should start with a capital letter"));
    }
    let number = chars.as_str();
    if number.is_empty() || number.len() > 2 || !number.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_digit()) {
        return Err(format!("{s:?} needs one or two digits after the letter"));
    }
    Ok(s.to_string())
}
  • #[derive(Parser)] writes the parser. #[arg(long)] makes a field a --name value option.
  • A plain String field is required. Option<String> is optional. default_value fills it in when it's left out.
  • value_parser = parse_shelf runs your function on the raw text. Its Err message goes into clap's error, so the user sees exactly what was wrong.
  • A parser can return a type of your own instead of a String, such as a small Month. clap then needs that type to be Clone, and says so: "the trait bound `Month: Clone` is not satisfied". #[derive(Clone)] on it is the fix.

In a real program you call Cli::parse(), which reads the real arguments and exits on error. To see the results here, the examples use Cli::try_parse_from, which takes the arguments as a list and returns a Result instead:

let args = ["fines", "--shelf", "B12", "--member", "Grace"];
let cli = Cli::try_parse_from(args).expect("good arguments");
println!("{cli:?}");
Cli { shelf: "B12", member: Some("Grace"), out: "out/fines.xlsx" }

And three things a person might type wrong:

for args in [
    vec!["fines", "--shelf", "b12"],
    vec!["fines", "--shelf", "B123"],
    vec!["fines", "--member", "Grace"],
] {
    let err = Cli::try_parse_from(&args).unwrap_err();
    print!("{err}");
    println!("(exit code {})\n", err.exit_code());
}
error: invalid value 'b12' for '--shelf <SHELF>': "b12" should start with a capital letter

For more information, try '--help'.
(exit code 2)

error: invalid value 'B123' for '--shelf <SHELF>': "B123" needs one or two digits after the letter

For more information, try '--help'.
(exit code 2)

error: the following required arguments were not provided:
  --shelf <SHELF>

Usage: fines --shelf <SHELF> --member <MEMBER>

For more information, try '--help'.
(exit code 2)

Every one of those messages came from clap, using your parse_shelf text for the first two. The exit code 2 is the Unix convention for "you used the command wrongly". The help text is free too, and stays in step with the code because it is generated from it. This is what --help prints:

Fines report for the lending library

Usage: fines [OPTIONS] --shelf <SHELF>

Options:
      --shelf <SHELF>    Shelf to report on: one capital letter and one or two digits, like B12
      --member <MEMBER>  Only this member's fines
      --out <OUT>        Where to write the workbook [default: out/fines.xlsx]
  -h, --help             Print help

The usage lines say fines because of #[command(name = "fines")] and because the examples pass "fines" as the first argument. Run your own program with cargo run -- --help and the usage line names the program that's actually running, such as snippets or kettle_creek.

Validating in the parser has a second benefit. Once Cli exists, its shelf is a well-formed shelf code. Code further in never has to check again, the same idea as parsing Millbrook's rows into proper types in ticket 4.

Writing a workbook

use rusqlite::Connection;
use rust_xlsxwriter::{Format, FormatBorder, Workbook, XlsxError};

/// A fine in whole cents, as in ticket 3.
struct Fine {
    loan_id: i64,
    cents: i64,
}

fn fines(db: &Connection) -> rusqlite::Result<Vec<Fine>> {
    let mut stmt = db.prepare("SELECT loan_id, amount FROM fines")?;
    let rows = stmt.query_map([], |r| {
        let dollars: f64 = r.get(1)?;
        Ok(Fine {
            loan_id: r.get(0)?,
            cents: (dollars * 100.0).round() as i64,
        })
    })?;
    rows.collect()
}

fn write_fines(path: &str, fines: &[Fine]) -> Result<(), XlsxError> {
    let mut workbook = Workbook::new();
    let header = Format::new()
        .set_bold()
        .set_border_bottom(FormatBorder::Thin);
    let money = Format::new().set_num_format("$#,##0.00;[Red]($#,##0.00)");

    let sheet = workbook.add_worksheet();
    sheet.set_name("Fines")?;
    sheet.write_string_with_format(0, 0, "Loan", &header)?;
    sheet.write_string_with_format(0, 1, "Amount", &header)?;
    for (i, fine) in fines.iter().enumerate() {
        let row = i as u32 + 1;
        sheet.write_number(row, 0, fine.loan_id as f64)?;
        sheet.write_number_with_format(row, 1, fine.cents as f64 / 100.0, &money)?;
    }
    sheet.set_column_width(0, 8)?;
    sheet.set_column_width(1, 14)?;
    sheet.set_freeze_panes(1, 0)?;
    sheet.autofilter(0, 0, fines.len() as u32, 1)?;

    workbook.save(path)
}
let mut all = fines(&db)?;
all.push(Fine {
    loan_id: 4,
    cents: -30,
}); // a refund
write_fines("library_fines.xlsx", &all)?;
let size = std::fs::metadata("library_fines.xlsx")?.len();
println!(
    "wrote library_fines.xlsx: {} fines, {} KB",
    all.len(),
    size / 1024
);
wrote library_fines.xlsx: 7 fines, 5 KB
  • Rows and columns are zero-based numbers: row 0, column 0 is cell A1. Rows are u32 and columns are u16, because a sheet has at most 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns, so as u32 on a loop index is normal here.
  • write_number stores a number. Excel numbers are f64, so your Cents becomes dollars at the last possible moment, for display only. All the adding up has already happened in integers. Writing a formatted string like "$1,204.50" instead would look the same and break Priya's SUM, which is the mistake the email is warning you about.
  • A Format is made once and passed by reference to every cell that uses it. "$#,##0.00;[Red]($#,##0.00)" is Excel's own number format language: the part before the semicolon is for positive numbers, the part after for negatives, here red and in parentheses, the accountants' convention.
  • set_freeze_panes(1, 0) freezes everything above row 1, so the header stays put when scrolling. autofilter takes the first and last row and column of the table, header included.
  • Almost every method returns a Result, because almost anything can be invalid: a sheet name over 31 characters, a row past the limit. ? handles all of them.

Failing like a good citizen

A program run by a person can print an error and stop. A program run by a scheduler has to say whether it worked in a way another program can check, and that's the exit status: 0 for success, anything else for failure. main can return std::process::ExitCode to choose it:

use clap::Parser;
use std::process::ExitCode;

#[derive(Parser)]
#[command(name = "fines")]
struct Cli {
    /// The library database
    #[arg(long, default_value = "library.db")]
    db: String,
}

fn run(cli: &Cli) -> Result<usize, String> {
    if !std::path::Path::new(&cli.db).exists() {
        return Err(format!("database not found: {}", cli.db));
    }
    // A stand-in for the real work: this example is about exit codes,
    // so it only checks the file exists and reports a made-up count.
    Ok(7)
}

fn real_main() -> ExitCode {
    let cli = Cli::parse(); // bad arguments: clap prints why and exits with 2
    match run(&cli) {
        Ok(n) => {
            println!("wrote {n} fines");
            ExitCode::SUCCESS
        }
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("error: {e}");
            ExitCode::FAILURE // exit status 1
        }
    }
}

The example's function is called real_main only because the program that tested it for this page needed main for itself. In your program it is fn main() -> ExitCode.

run is a stand-in: it checks the file exists and reports a made-up count, because the point here is the exit status. To try it in snippets, make an empty file to point it at first, with touch library.db. Run from a shell, with echo $? printing the last exit status:

$ fines --db library.db
wrote 7 fines
$ echo $?
0

$ fines --db missing.db
error: database not found: missing.db
$ echo $?
1

$ fines --month 2026-08
error: unexpected argument '--month' found

Usage: fines [OPTIONS]

For more information, try '--help'.
$ echo $?
2

Three outcomes, three statuses. eprintln! writes to standard error instead of standard output, which is where error messages belong. Under the hood explains why the difference matters. Returning Result from main, as you have been, also exits with 1 on Err. ExitCode gives you control of the message and the number.

The ticket

One decision before you start: what plain cargo run does now. If --month is required, it stops with exit status 2, and ticket 5's cargo run && diff line stops with it. Either make --month an Option, so tickets 1 to 5 still come out of a plain cargo run and the pack is written only when a month is given, or keep it required and run cargo run -- --month 2026-09 from now on, with the new workbook expected in any diff. Both are fine. Say which in your journal and in your hand-in.

Before you type, answer these in your journal. What does each table sheet's row type need to carry, and does it own its data or borrow it from the vectors you loaded? Your ticket 5 code produced CSVs: which of its functions can the pack call as they are, and which return the wrong shape? Is --month a String once it's been checked, or would a small type of its own be clearer? Where does the decision "this run failed" get turned into an exit status, and is there exactly one such place?

Stuck?

Hint 1: the shape of the trait

The wiki's cells returns Vec<String>, which loses the difference between text and numbers. Your sheets need that difference, because money must be written with write_number_with_format. So let the row write itself: a method that takes the worksheet, the row number and the money format, and writes its own cells. Its signature can look like fn write_row(&self, sheet: &mut Worksheet, row: u32, money: &Format) -> Result<(), XlsxError>. The &mut is what lets it write cells, and workbook.add_worksheet() is where a &mut Worksheet comes from. The generic function writes the header, then calls write_row once per row with a row number one past the last.

Hint 2: rows that borrow

A discrepancy row needs the supplier's name, which lives in your suppliers Vec. Rather than cloning every name into a new struct, a small struct with a &'a Discrepancy and a &'a str can implement the trait. Implementing a trait for a type with a lifetime looks like impl TableRow for DiscrepancyRow<'_>. The '_ means "some lifetime, and I don't need to name it", because nothing in the impl has to say how it relates to anything else. Most of the time Rust works lifetimes out without being told, and '_ marks a spot where you let it.

Hint 3: no half-finished file

Do all the loading, parsing and reconciling first, and build the Workbook in memory. save is the only call that touches the output file, so if anything before it fails, nothing is written. Validate the month in clap's value_parser, and it fails before the database is even opened.

Sanity checks

  • The sheet tabs read Summary, Spend, Discrepancies, Rejects, left to right.
  • The Summary's count of invoices dated in September is under 150, and September's spend is well under the Q3 total from ticket 2.
  • The Discrepancies sheet has as many data rows as your ticket 5 discrepancies.csv, and the Rejects sheet as many as your rejects.csv.
  • Select the Total column on the Spend sheet in a spreadsheet. The status bar shows a sum. If it shows only a count, the numbers went in as text.
  • cargo run -- --month 2026-13; echo $? prints an error and a non-zero number, and ls out/ shows no new workbook.

One exception to the "same output, byte for byte" rule from the review checklist: a workbook records the moment it was created, in docProps/core.xml, so two runs of a correct program give files with different checksums. Either compare what's in the sheets, or pin the timestamp. Look up DocProperties::set_creation_datetime and Workbook::set_properties in the rust_xlsxwriter docs, and decide whether a fixed date in the file is honest.

Under the hood

Generics and trait objects, compiled

When you call print_table(&books) and print_table(&loans), the compiler writes two copies of print_table, one with T replaced by Book and one by Loan. That's monomorphization, from "one shape". Each copy calls its type's cells directly, and the optimizer can inline it as if you'd written two separate functions by hand. The price is size and build time: a generic used with fifty types is compiled fifty times. (The optimizer may then inline some copies into their callers or merge identical ones, so the final count can be lower.) This is static dispatch, because which method runs is fixed when the program is compiled.

A trait object works the other way. The compiler builds one table per type, the vtable, listing that type's implementation of each method, and a &dyn Describe carries two pointers: one to the value and one to its type's vtable. A method call reads the function's address out of the vtable and jumps there. You can see the second pointer:

use std::mem::size_of;

println!("&Book:          {} bytes", size_of::<&Book>());
println!("&dyn Describe:  {} bytes", size_of::<&dyn Describe>());
println!(
    "Box<dyn Describe>: {} bytes",
    size_of::<Box<dyn Describe>>()
);
&Book:          8 bytes
&dyn Describe:  16 bytes
Box<dyn Describe>: 16 bytes

A fat pointer, twice the size of an ordinary reference. This is dynamic dispatch: one copy of the code, decided at run time. The optimizer usually can't see through the jump to inline it, though it sometimes works out which method it must be. For a monthly report, the speed difference between the two is far too small to measure. Choose by what the code needs to say: a fixed type per call means generics, a mixed collection means dyn. C++ templates and virtual functions make the same trade. In Java and Python, calling a method on a value of a generic type always looks the method up at run time: Java's compiler erases the type parameter, and Python looks up every method as it runs. So their generics never get Rust's per-type copies.

An .xlsx file is a folder of XML

Office Open XML, the format behind .xlsx, .docx and .pptx, is a ZIP archive of XML files. A one-fine workbook made the same way as the wiki's example, listed with unzip -l (dates and times blanked here):

  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
     1167  (date)             [Content_Types].xml
      587  (date)             _rels/.rels
      697  (date)             xl/_rels/workbook.xml.rels
     6995  (date)             xl/theme/theme1.xml
     1029  (date)             xl/styles.xml
      549  (date)             xl/workbook.xml
      636  (date)             xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml
      201  (date)             xl/sharedStrings.xml
      592  (date)             docProps/core.xml
      783  (date)             docProps/app.xml
---------                     -------
    13236                     10 files

Each sheet is its own XML file, and unzip -p prints one file from the archive: unzip -p library_fines.xlsx xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml. Here is the data section from a one-row workbook made the same way, with one fine of 24.95:

<sheetData>
  <row r="1" spans="1:2"><c r="A1" t="s"><v>0</v></c><c r="B1" t="s"><v>1</v></c></row>
  <row r="2" spans="1:2"><c r="A2"><v>6</v></c><c r="B2" s="1"><v>24.95</v></c></row>
</sheetData>

B2 holds the number 24.95 with style 1, the currency format, which lives in styles.xml. Cells with t="s" hold no text at all, only an index into sharedStrings.xml, where each distinct string is stored once:

<si><t>Loan</t></si><si><t>Amount</t></si>

A sheet with ten thousand rows of the same supplier names stores each name once. That's a decades-old compression trick called interning, and ZIP then compresses the XML on top. Run unzip -l on your own pack. Look at a sheet's XML, and find your money: it's a plain number, which is why Priya can sum it. The format is an open standard, ECMA-376, so any program can read your pack, not just Excel.

Processes, streams and exit codes

Every program starts with three open streams: standard input, standard output and standard error. println! writes to standard output and eprintln! to standard error. In a terminal they both appear on screen, which is why they look the same. They go to different places as soon as anything is redirected: cargo run -- --month 2026-09 > log.txt sends output to the file and still shows errors on screen, and a scheduler can save each to its own log. Data on one stream and complaints on the other is what lets programs be chained with pipes without errors getting mixed into the data.

When a process ends it hands its parent one small number, the exit status. Shells keep it in $?, and && and || act on it: cargo run -- --month 2026-09 && echo sent only says "sent" on success. Cron, systemd, CI servers and every job scheduler in Part 2 decide success or failure by this number alone. They never read your message. A program that prints "error" and exits 0 has told the scheduler everything went fine. Conventions: 0 is success, 1 is a general failure, 2 is bad usage (clap's choice, and many Unix tools'), and a few higher numbers are reserved by shells, so stay below 126.

Go deeper

  • The Rust Programming Language, chapter 10: Generic Types, Traits, and Lifetimes, especially 10.2 on traits.
  • Chapter 18.2: Using Trait Objects to Abstract over Shared Behavior, for dyn and the dyn compatibility rules.
  • Chapter 12: An I/O Project, a command-line program built from scratch with no crates. Worth reading to see what clap is doing for you, including the stderr discussion in 12.6.
  • clap's derive tutorial: subcommands, flags, possible values and validation.
  • rust_xlsxwriter's docs. Its examples cover charts, tables, conditional formats and formulas, if Priya asks for more.
  • The Rust API Guidelines: how the standard library and good crates name things, which traits types should implement, and why. Read the checklist page once you have a module others call.
  • The ExitCode docs, and std::process::Termination, which is how main can return either a Result or an ExitCode.
  • ECMA-376, the Office Open XML standard. Thousands of pages. Skim the part on SpreadsheetML to see how much a "simple" file format contains.
  • Rust for Rustaceans by Jon Gjengset, chapter 2 (Types) on dispatch and chapter 3 (Designing Interfaces) on choosing traits. The best book on writing Rust other people use, best read after part 2.

The bookshelf

You asked how to learn this properly rather than from a pile of mediocre tutorials. The honest answer is to use few sources, all of them primary: the official books, the standard library's docs, docs written by a crate's own author, and a handful of books by people who build these systems. Skip "Rust in an hour" videos, posts written before the 2018 edition, and any tutorial you can't trace to someone who ships Rust. Here is the shelf, in roughly the order it becomes useful.

Rust

The Rust Programming Language, Klabnik, Nichols and Krycho (free online)
The official book. Each ticket's "Go deeper" points at the chapters it just made you need. Read them then, not before.
The standard library docs
Better written than most books. When you wonder whether something exists, it's usually a method on Option, Iterator or str.
Rust by Example (free online)
Small runnable programs, one feature at a time. Good for "show me the syntax" moments.
Programming Rust, 2nd edition, Blandy, Orendorff and Tindall (O'Reilly, 2021)
The best second book. Deeper than the official one on ownership, traits, iterators and collections, written by systems programmers for systems programmers. Read it during part 1 and 2.
Rust for Rustaceans, Jon Gjengset (No Starch, 2021)
How experienced Rust developers think: API design, testing, error handling at scale, what unsafe is for. Read it after part 2, when your code has enough shape to be worth arguing about.
Zero to Production in Rust, Luca Palmieri (self-published)
Building and testing a real web service. It uses actix-web rather than the axum you'll use in part 3, but its habits (tests first, configuration, structured logging, error types) are what matter. Part 3's companion.
Rust Atomics and Locks, Mara Bos (O'Reilly, 2023, free online)
Concurrency from the hardware up, by a member of the Rust library team. For parts 2 and 3.
The Rust API Guidelines and the Clippy lint list
What idiomatic means, written down. Read a few clippy lint explanations a week: each one is a small lesson about why.

Software design

A Philosophy of Software Design, John Ousterhout (Yaknyam Press, 2nd edition 2021)
Short and opinionated, about the thing your reviews keep circling: how to split a program into pieces that hide their complexity. If you read one book on design, read this one, after ticket 5.
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly)
How real data systems handle failure, duplicates, ordering and time. Part 2's tickets are small versions of its chapters.

Computer science

Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, 3rd edition, Bryant and O'Hallaron (Pearson, 2015)
Memory, caches, linking, processes, networking: everything underneath your program, explained for the person writing it. Ticket 8 leans on chapter 6.
Introduction to Algorithms, 4th edition, Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein (MIT Press, 2022)
The reference. Dip in, don't read it cover to cover. The Algorithm Design Manual by Steven Skiena is the friendlier companion.
"What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic", David Goldberg (1991)
The paper behind ticket 3. Heavy going in places, and with your math background, the most rewarding thing on this list.
Numerical Linear Algebra, Trefethen and Bau (SIAM, 1997)
For part 4: why the textbook formula for least squares is the wrong one to compute with, and what to do instead.

Exam
